nodes.name: Hochschild complex via self-duality
nodes.statement: The Hochschild complex of an associative algebra is usually constructed as the totalization of a {\em simplicial} $\mathbf{k}$-vector space. This simplicial object can be obtained by precomposing the functor ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \to \operatorname{Vect}$ from Theorem \ref{thm:hochschild} with \[ \Delta^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \overset{D}{\longrightarrow} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \] where $D$ denotes a self-duality of the category ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ (cf. Corollary \ref{cor:duality} below).

nodes.name: Category of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-vector spaces
nodes.statement: We denote by ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}$ the category of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-vector spaces.

nodes.name: Constant $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-vector space
nodes.statement:
Let $\underline{\mathbf{k}}$ be the constant
${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-vector space with stalk $\mathbf{k}$, i.e., the contravariant functor which takes each object to $\mathbf{k}$
and each morphism to the identity.

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-homology and cohomology
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be a unital associative algebra with a twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action. By Theorem
\ref{thm:hochschild}, $C_\bullet(A)$ is an object of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}$. Following the approach of Connes
and Loday, we define the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-{\em homology} and {\em cohomology} of $A$ to be
\begin{align*}
H_\bullet^{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(A) & = \operatorname{Tor}_\bullet^{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}}( \mathbf{k}, C_\bullet(A)),\\
H^\bullet_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(A) & = \operatorname{Ext}^\bullet_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}}(  C_\bullet(A), \mathbf{k}) 
\end{align*}
where $\mathbf{k}$ denotes the constant ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-module.

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-trace
nodes.statement: Elements of $H^0_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}(A) = \operatorname{Hom}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Vect}}( C_\bullet(A), \mathbf{k})$ will be called {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-traces} on $A$. Thus a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-trace $\beta$ is a collection of multilinear forms $\beta_n: A^{\otimes(n+1)}, \mathbf{k})$, $n\geq 0$. The condition that $\beta$ is a morphism of cosimplicial vector spaces, means that all the $\beta_n$ are expressible through the linear form $\beta_1$: \[ \beta_n(a_0, a_1, \cdots, a_n) = \beta_1(a_0a_1\cdots a_n). \] The further conditions on $\beta_1$ express $\mathfrak{G}_n$-invariance of $\beta_n$ for $n\geq 0$. Note that these conditions do not necessarily imply that the bilinear form $\beta_2$ is symmetric.

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-Frobenius algebra
nodes.statement: A {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Frobenius algebra} is a finite-dimensional unital associative algebra $A$ equipped with a twisted $\mathfrak{G}_0$-action and a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-trace $\beta$ such that the bilinear form $\beta_2$ is non-degenerate.

nodes.name: Connes' cyclic structure on the Hochschild complex
nodes.statement:
The fact that $\operatorname{NC}_\bullet{\EuScript C}$ is cyclic,
corresponds to the fundamental observation of Connes that $C_\bullet (A)$ has a natural structure of
a cyclic vector space. In this structure, the generator $\tau_n$ of $\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)=\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits \langle n \rangle$ acts by
cyclic rotation
\[
\tau_n(a_0\otimes  \cdots \otimes  a_n) \,\,=\,\,  a_n\otimes a_0\otimes  \cdots \otimes a_{n-1}.
\]

nodes.name: $\Lambda$-traces and $\Lambda$-Frobenius algebras are classical
nodes.statement:
The concept of a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-trace on $A$ reduces, for ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}=\Lambda$, to  that of a linear functional
$\beta_1:A\to\mathbf{k}$ such that for each $n$ the multilinear form $\beta_1(a_0\cdots a_n)$ is cyclically
symmetric. As well known, this is equivalent to requiring that $\beta_1(ab)=\beta_1(ba)$, so
$\beta_1$ is the trace in the classical sense and $\beta_2$ is an invariant symmetric bilinear form
on $A$. Further, the concept of a $\Lambda$-Frobenius algebra reduces to the classical one: a not
necessarily commutative, associative unital $\mathbf{k}$-algebra with a trace $\beta_1$ such that
$\beta_1(ab)$ is a nondenerate bilinear form.

nodes.name: Loday's dihedral structure on the Hochschild complex
nodes.statement:
Let $(A,*)$ be a unital associative algebra
with involution. As observed by Loday \cite[\S 5.2.11]{loday} $C_\bullet (A)$ becomes a dihedral
vector space, with $\omega_n$ acting by 
\[
  \omega_n(a_0\otimes  \cdots \otimes a_n) \,\,=\,\,  a_0^*\otimes a_n^*\otimes a_{n-1}^*\otimes
  \cdots \otimes a_2^* \otimes a_1^*. 
\]
assumptions: Let $(A,*)$ be a unital associative algebra

nodes.name: $\Xi$-traces
nodes.statement:
A $\Xi$-trace on $A$ is a linear functional $\beta_1:A\to\mathbf{k}$ satisfying the identities
\[
	\beta_1(a^*)=\beta_1(a), \quad  \beta_1(ab) = \beta_1(ba),
\] 
which imply that $\beta_1(ab)=\beta_1(a^*b^*)$, i.e., that the involution preserves the bilinear
form $\beta_2$ (as well as all the higher $\beta_n$).

nodes.name: Twisted Hochschild complex is paracyclic
nodes.statement:
Suppose
$A$ is  a unital associative algebra equipped with an automorphism $F$. We then have an invertible
transformation $\tau_n$ on $C_n(A)$ given by
\begin{equation} \tau_n(a_0, \cdots, a_n) = (F^{-1} (a_n), a_0, a_1, \cdots, a_{n-1}). 
\end{equation}
This makes $C_\bullet(A)$ into a paracyclic vector space. If $F^N=\operatorname{Id}$ for some $N$, then
$C_\bullet(A)$ is an $N$-cyclic vector space.
assumptions:
Suppose
$A$ is  a unital associative algebra equipped with an automorphism $F$.
If $F^N=\operatorname{Id}$ for some $N$
conclusions: This makes $C_\bullet(A)$ into a paracyclic vector space.

nodes.name: Twisted cyclic operator on $C_n(A)$
nodes.statement: \tau_n(a_0, \cdots, a_n) = (F^{-1} (a_n), a_0, a_1, \cdots, a_{n-1}).
nodes.label: eq:tau-tw-alg

nodes.name: $\Lambda_\infty$-traces
nodes.statement:
A $\Lambda_\infty$-trace on $A$ is a linear functional $\beta_1: A\to\mathbf{k}$ such that
\[
	\beta_1(F(a))=\beta_1(a), \quad  \beta_1(a\cdot b) = \beta_1(b\cdot F(a)). 
\]
In particular, the form $\beta_2(a,b)=\beta_1(ab)$ is not required to be symmetric, and $F$
intertwines $\beta_2$ and $\beta_2^t$:
\begin{equation} \beta_2(a,b) = \beta_2(b, F(a)). 
\end{equation}

nodes.name: Nakayama relation
nodes.statement: \beta_2(a,b) = \beta_2(b, F(a)).
nodes.label: eq:nakayama

nodes.name: Nakayama automorphism
nodes.statement:
Note that in the Frobenius case ($A$ finite-dimensional and $\beta_2$, considered as a morphism
$A\to A^*$, is an isomorphism), $F$ is defined by \eqref{eq:nakayama} uniquely:
$F=\beta_2^{-1}\beta_2^t$. In this context $F$ is called the {\em Nakayama automorphism} of
$\beta_2$.

nodes.name: $\Lambda_\infty$- and $\Lambda_N$-Frobenius algebras
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] A $\Lambda_\infty$-Frobenius algebra is the same as a finite-dimensional unital associative algebra $A$ together with a linear functional $\beta_1: A\to\mathbf{k}$ such that: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a1)] $\beta_2(a,b)=\beta_1(ab)$ is a non-degenerate, not necessarily symmetric bilinear form on $A$. \item[(a2)] The Nakayama automorphism $F$ of $\beta_2$ is an algebra automorphism of $A$. \end{enumerate} \item[(b)] A $\Lambda_N$-Frobenius algebra is a $\Lambda_\infty$-Frobenius algebra such that $F^N=\operatorname{Id}\nolimits$. \end{enumerate} \qed
nodes.statement_short: A $\Lambda_\infty$-Frobenius algebra is a finite-dimensional algebra with nondegenerate form whose Nakayama automorphism is an algebra automorphism; $\Lambda_N$ adds $F^N=\mathrm{Id}$.

nodes.name: Quaternionic structure on the Hochschild complex
nodes.statement:
Let $A$ be an associative algebra with an anti-automorphism $J$ of order 4.
Then the transformation
\[
w_n(a_0\otimes \cdots \otimes a_n) \,\,=\,\, J^{-1}(a_0) \otimes J(a_n) \otimes \cdots \otimes J(a_1)
\]
together with $\tau_n$ defined as in \eqref{eq:tau-tw-alg} for $F=J^2$, make $C_\bullet (A)$ into a
quaternionic object in the category of vector spaces.

nodes.name: $\nabla$-traces
nodes.statement:
A $\nabla$-trace on $A$ is a linear functional $\beta: A\to\mathbf{k}$ such  that $\beta_1(Ja) = \beta_1(a)$
and $\beta_2(a,b)=\beta_1(ab)$ satisfies the conditions:
\[
	\beta_2(a,b) = \beta_2(b, J^2 a) = \beta_2(J^{-1} a, Jb).
\]

nodes.name: Expected TQFTs from $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-Frobenius algebras
nodes.statement: (a) Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be any planar simplicial group with corresponding planar Lie group $\mathbb{G}$. We expect that the theory of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs developed in \S \ref{sec:structuredgraphs} can be used to generalize the results of \cite{kock, alex-natanzon, novak-runkel} as follows: A ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Frobenius algebra gives rise to a numerical invariant defined on $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces without boundary and to a TQFT on $\mathbb{G}$-structured 2-dimensional cobordisms (with marked points as in \S \ref{subsec:c-infty} allowed in both cases and with additional constraints of commutativity removing the dependence on marking points). \vskip .1cm (b) Further, one can extend the concept of a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Frobenius algebra to the case of associative dg (or $A_{\infty}$) algebras, and dg (or $A_\infty$) categories also allowing the forms $\beta_1$ and $\beta_2$ to have some degree $d\neq 0$ as in \cite{kontsevich-feynman}. The corresponding ``$d$-dimensional ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-Calabi-Yau algebras and categories" should then give cohomology classes on moduli spaces of marked $\mathbb{G}$-structured surfaces generalizing \cite{costello-TFT, kontsevich-feynman}. We leave both these directions to future work.

nodes.name: Category $\mathcal{G}$ of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structured sets (diagram)
Structured sets diagram
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \ar[d]_\lambda \ar[r]^\epsilon& {\mathcal G} \ar[d]^{\lambda_{{\mathcal G}}}\\ {\bf N}\ar[r]& {\bf FSet} }
nodes.label: eq:Gc

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structured set
nodes.statement: Let ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ be a crossed simplicial group. A {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set} is a pair $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$, where: \begin{enumerate} \item[(1)] $I$ is a nonempty finite set of some cardinality $n+1$, $n\geq 0$. \item[(2)] $\mathcal{O}(I)$ is a right $\mathfrak{G}_n$-torsor together with a map \[ \rho: \mathcal{O}(I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}\bigl( \{0,1,\dots, n\}, I \bigr) \] which is equivariant with respect to the homomorphism $\lambda_n: \mathfrak{G}_n\to S_{n+1}$ from Proposition \ref {prop:forget}. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-order
nodes.statement: The datum of $\rho$ will be referred to as a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-{\em structure}, or a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-{\em order}, on the set $I$.

nodes.name: Structured frames
nodes.statement: Elements of $\mathcal{O}(I)$ will be called {\em structured frames} of $I$.

nodes.name: Morphisms of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structured sets
nodes.statement: A morphism of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets \[ \psi: (I', \mathcal{O}(I'))\longrightarrow (I, \mathcal{O}(I)), \quad |I'|=n'+1, \, |I|=n+1, \] is a datum of morphisms \[ \left\{ \psi_{f,f'}\in\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([n'], [n]) \; \big| \; \text{$f'\in \mathcal{O}(I')$, $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$}\right\}, \] satisfying, for every $g \in \mathfrak{G}_{n}$, $g' \in \mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, the equivariance condition \[ \psi_{fg, f'g'} = g^{-1} \circ \psi_{f, f'}\circ g'. \] The composition of two morphisms \[ (I'', \mathcal{O}(I'')) \overset{\psi'}{\longrightarrow} (I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \overset{\psi}{\longrightarrow} (I, \mathcal{O}(I)) \] is defined by the formula \[ (\psi\psi')_{f, f''} = \psi_{f,f'} \circ \psi'_{f', f''} \] where the right hand is independent on $f'$.
nodes.label: defi:dgstructure

nodes.name: Category $\mathcal{G}$
nodes.statement: We denote by $\mathcal{G}$ the category of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets thus defined.

nodes.name: Proof of $\mathcal{G}$ is equivalent to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$
nodes.statement:
The following is then
immediate.
nodes.statement_short: Immediate from the definitions.

nodes.name: $\mathcal{G}$ is equivalent to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] We have an equivalence of categories $\epsilon:{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}\to\mathcal{G}$ sending an object $[n]$ to the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set $(\{0,1,\dots, n\}, \mathfrak{G}_n)$. \item[(b)] For any object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))\in\mathcal{G}$, we have a canonical identification of $\mathfrak{G}_n$-torsors \[ \mathcal{O}(I) \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Isom}_{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon [n], (I, \mathcal{O}(I))) \] and of sets \[ I \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}}(\epsilon[0], (I, \mathcal{O}(I))/\mathfrak{G}_0. \] \item[(c)] In particular, the correspondence $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))\mapsto I$ gives a functor $ \lambda_{\mathcal{G}}:\mathcal{G}\to {\bf FSet}$ extending $\lambda:{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}\to\bf N$. \qed \end{itemize}
conclusions: We have an equivalence of categories
we have a canonical identification of

nodes.name: Groupoid $\mathcal{G}/I$ of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-orders
nodes.statement: Let $I$ be a nonempty finite set. The category $\mathcal{G}/I$ of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-orders on $I$ has objects given by all ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structures on $I$, and morphisms given by those morphisms $\psi: (I,\mathcal{O})\to (I, \mathcal{O}')$ in $\mathcal{G}$ which induce the identity map on the set $I$.

nodes.name: Number of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-orders on a set
nodes.statement:
Clearly, $\mathcal{G}/I$ is a groupoid. If $|I|=n+1$ and $|\mathfrak{G}_n|<\infty$, then the number of isomorphism
classes of objects of $\mathcal{G}/I$ is
\[
|\pi_0(\mathcal{G}/I)| = \frac{(n+1)!}{|\mathfrak{G}_n|} \cdot |\mathfrak{G}_n^0|, \quad \text{where
$\mathfrak{G}_n^0=\operatorname{Ker}\nolimits(\lambda_n)$.} 
\]
This number can be understood as ``the number of different ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-orders on $I$". Each such order,
represented by an object of $\mathcal{G}/I$, has automorphism group isomorphic to $\mathfrak{G}_n^0$.
assumptions: If $|I|=n+1$ and $|\mathfrak{G}_n|<\infty$

nodes.name: Dihedral orders on small sets
nodes.statement: Consider the crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}} = \Xi$ given by the dihedral category. We have $\mathfrak{G}_0 = \mathfrak{G}_0^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ so that, for a singleton set $I$, the category $\mathcal{G}/I$ has a single isomorphism class of objects and each object has automorphism group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. We have $\mathfrak{G}_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z} \times \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ and $\mathfrak{G}_1^0 = \mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$ so that, on a given set $I$ of cardinality $2$, we have one isomorphism class of objects in $\mathcal{G}/I$, each object having automorphism group $\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$. For $|I| = n+1$ with $n \ge 2$, the objects of $\mathcal{G}/I$ have trivial automorphism group, and there are $\frac{n!}{2}$ isomorphism classes.

nodes.name: Morphisms of structured sets as pairs $(\psi_*,\psi^*)$
nodes.statement: The set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}}((I', \mathcal{O}(I')), (I, \mathcal{O}(I)))$ is in bijection with the set of pairs $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$, where $\psi_*: I'\to I$ and $\psi^*: \mathcal{O}(I)\to\mathcal{O}(I')$ are maps of sets such that: \begin{itemize} \item[(i)] For every structured frame $f$ of $I$, the unique map $f^*\psi: \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\to \{0,1,\dots, n\}$ making the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots,n'\} \ar[d]_{\rho(\psi^*f)}\ar[r]^{f^*\psi }& \{0,1,\dots,n\} \ar[d]^{\rho(f)} \\ I'\ar[r]_{\psi_*}&I } \] commutative is given by a morphism in $\Delta$. \item[(ii)] For each frame $f$ of $I$ and $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$, we have \[ \psi^*(f . g) = \psi^*(f) . (f^*\psi)^*(g), \] where $(f^*\psi)^*: \mathfrak{G}_n\to\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$ is the map associated to $f^*\psi$ via the simplicial set $\mathfrak{G}$. \end{itemize}
nodes.statement_short: Morphisms of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structured sets correspond to a map of sets and a map of frames satisfying monotonicity and an equivariance identity.
conclusions: is in bijection with the set of pairs
nodes.label: prop:morphisms-Gc

nodes.name: Proof of Morphisms of structured sets as pairs $(\psi_*,\psi^*)$
nodes.statement: Let $\psi=(\psi_{f,f'})$ be a morphism from $(I', \mathcal{O}(I'))$ to $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ in $\mathcal{G}$. The map $\psi_*: I'\to I$ is defined to be the value, on $\psi$, of the functor $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$. To define the map $\psi^*: \mathcal{O}(I)\to\mathcal{O}(I')$ associated to $\psi$, we fix $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, choose and arbitrary $f'\in\mathcal{O}(I')$ and interpret them as vertical isomorphisms in the diagram \[ \xymatrix{ (I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \ar[rr]^\psi && (I, \mathcal{O}(I)) \\ \epsilon[n'] \ar[u]^{f'} \ar[rr]^{\psi_{f, f'} = f^{-1}\circ\psi\circ f' }&& \epsilon[n] \ar[u]_f \\\epsilon[n']\ar[u]^{g'} \ar[urr]_\phi } \] Next, we define $\phi$ and $g'$ in the diagram via the canonical factorization $\psi_{f, f'} = \phi\circ g'$ with $\phi\in\Delta$, $g'\in\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, and set $\psi^*(f)=f'\circ g'$. The result is independent of $f'$ in virtue of the equivariance condition on the datum $\psi=(\psi_{f, f'})$. This defines the pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ associated to $\psi$. We leave the remaining verifications to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_*$ via $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$ and $\psi^*$ via canonical factorization of $\psi_{f,f'}$; independence uses equivariance.

nodes.name: Define $\psi_*$ as the value of $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$.
nodes.statement:
Let $\psi=(\psi_{f,f'})$ be a morphism from $(I', \mathcal{O}(I'))$
to $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ in $\mathcal{G}$. The map $\psi_*: I'\to I$ is defined to be the value, on $\psi$,
of the functor $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi_*$ as the value of $\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}$.

nodes.name: Fix frames and set up the diagram.
nodes.statement:
To define the map $\psi^*: \mathcal{O}(I)\to\mathcal{O}(I')$ associated to $\psi$,
we fix $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, choose and arbitrary $f'\in\mathcal{O}(I')$ and interpret them as vertical
isomorphisms in the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
(I', \mathcal{O}(I')) \ar[rr]^\psi && (I, \mathcal{O}(I))
\\
\epsilon[n']
\ar[u]^{f'} 
 \ar[rr]^{\psi_{f, f'} = f^{-1}\circ\psi\circ f' }&& \epsilon[n]
 \ar[u]_f
 \\\epsilon[n']\ar[u]^{g'} 
 \ar[urr]_\phi
}
\]
nodes.statement_short: Fix frames and set up the diagram.

nodes.name: Define $\psi^*(f)$ via canonical factorization; independent of $f'$.
nodes.statement:
Next, we define $\phi$ and $g'$ in the diagram via the canonical factorization
$\psi_{f, f'} = \phi\circ g'$ with $\phi\in\Delta$, $g'\in\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$, and set $\psi^*(f)=f'\circ g'$. The result is independent
of $f'$ in virtue of the equivariance condition on the datum $\psi=(\psi_{f, f'})$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\psi^*(f)$ via canonical factorization; independent of $f'$.

nodes.name: The pair is defined; remaining checks left to reader.
nodes.statement:
This defines the pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ associated to $\psi$. We leave the remaining verifications
to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: The pair is defined; remaining checks left to reader.

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-closure of a linear order
nodes.statement: A linear order $\leq$ on a nonempty finite set $I$ defines a canonical ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-order on $I$ called the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-{\em closure} of $\leq$: Note that $\leq$ can be identified with the unique monotone bijection $\sigma: \{0,1,\dots, n\}\to I$, where $|I|= n+1$. We then define the $\mathfrak{G}_n$-torsor $\mathcal{O}_{\sigma}$ to be $\mathfrak{G}_n$, and the map $\rho$ to be the composition \[ \mathfrak{G}_n\buildrel\lambda_n\over\longrightarrow S_{n+1}= \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}\bigl( \{0,1,\dots, n\}, \{0,1,\dots, n\}\bigr)\buildrel\sigma_*\over\longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}\bigl( \{0,1,\dots, n\}, I\bigr). \] Denoting by ${\bf\Delta}$ the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, we can view the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure as a functor ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta} \to\mathcal{G}$ extending $i:\Delta \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.label: ex:DG-closure

nodes.name: Model of $\mathcal{G}/I$ via linear orders
nodes.statement: \begin{itemize} \item[(a)] For linear orders on $I$ given by bijections $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$, we have \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}/I}((I, \mathcal{O}_{\sigma_1}), (I, \mathcal{O}_{\sigma_2})) \cong \bigl\{ g\in\mathfrak{G}_n \bigl| \,\, \lambda_n(g) = \sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2\bigr\}, \] and the composition of morphisms corresponds to the multiplication in $\mathfrak{G}_n$. \item[(b)] Every object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ of $\mathcal{G}/I$ is isomorphic to an object of the form $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$, so the category with objects $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$ and morphisms defined by the right hand side of the identification in (a), is equivalent to $\mathcal{G}/I$. \end{itemize}
assumptions: For linear orders on $I$ given by bijections $\sigma_1, \sigma_2$
conclusions: and the composition of morphisms corresponds to the multiplication in $\mathfrak{G}_n$.
Every object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ of $\mathcal{G}/I$ is isomorphic to an object of the form $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$
nodes.label: prop:model-G/I

nodes.name: Proof of Model of $\mathcal{G}/I$ via linear orders
nodes.statement: (a) is straightforward from the definitions. To prove (b), note that any $f\in \mathcal{O}(I)$ gives rise to an isomorphism $\psi^f: [n]\to (I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ in $\mathcal{G}$ which gives a bijection $\sigma=\lambda(\psi^f)$ from $\{0,1,\dots, n\}$ to $I$. We then see easily that $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ is isomorphic to $(I, \mathcal{O}_\sigma)$ by an isomorphism identical on $I$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: (a) is direct; for (b) a frame gives a bijection $\sigma$ and an isomorphism with $(I,\mathcal{O}_\sigma)$.

nodes.name: Restriction of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structures
nodes.statement_short: An embedding $I'\hookrightarrow I$ induces a restriction functor $\mathcal{G}/I\to\mathcal{G}/I'$ with canonical morphisms, compatible with composition.
assumptions: Let $u: I'\hookrightarrow I$ be an embedding of nonempty finite sets.

nodes.name: Proof of Restriction of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-structures
nodes.statement_short: Restrict linear orders and use the canonical square to define $\operatorname{Res}$ on morphisms by $g\mapsto\phi_1^*(g)$; functoriality from the crossed identity.

nodes.name: Use the linear-order model and define $\operatorname{Res}$ on objects.
nodes.statement_short: Use the linear-order model and define $\operatorname{Res}$ on objects.

nodes.name: Restriction square
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\sigma'} \ar[r]^\phi& \{0,1, \dots, n\}\ar[d]^\sigma \\ I'\ar[r]_u& I, }
nodes.label: eq:comm-diagr-emb

nodes.name: Two orders and their restricted diagrams.
nodes.statement:
Further, let $g\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ be such that $\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2$, where 
$\sigma_1, \sigma_2: \{0,1, \dots, n\}\to I$ are the bijections corresponding to two total orders
$\leq^1, \leq^2$ on $I$. Let $\sigma'_1, \sigma'_2: \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\to I'$ be the
bijections corresponding to the restrictions of $\leq^1, \leq^2$ to $I'$. We the have two commutative
diagrams as in \eqref{eq:comm-diagr-emb}, whose arrows we denote $u, \sigma'_\nu, \sigma_\nu, \phi_\nu$,
$\nu=1,2$.
nodes.statement_short: Two orders and their restricted diagrams.

nodes.name: Claim $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$
nodes.statement_short: Show $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$ via the canonical square.

nodes.name: Apply $\lambda$ to the canonical square.
nodes.statement:
Indeed, consider the canonical diagram in ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$
\[
\xymatrix{
[n']\ar[d]_{\phi_1^*g}
\ar[r]^{g^*\phi_1}&[n]
\ar[d]^g
\\
[n']\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& [n]
}
\]
defining $g^*\phi_1$ and apply the functor $\lambda$ to it.
nodes.statement_short: Apply $\lambda$ to the canonical square.

nodes.name: The resulting square gives $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.
nodes.statement_short: The resulting square gives $\phi_2=g^*\phi_1$.

nodes.name: Image of the canonical square
nodes.statement: \xymatrix{ \{0,1,\dots, n'\} \ar[d]_{\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)} \ar[r]^{\phi_2}& \{0,1,\dots, n\} \ar[d]^{\lambda_n(g)=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma^2} \\ \{0,1,\dots, n'\}\ar[r]_{\phi_1}& \{0,1,\dots, n\}, }
nodes.label: eq:2.1.11

nodes.name: Uniqueness gives $\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)=(\sigma_1')^{-1}\sigma_2'$.
nodes.statement:
We further claim that
$\lambda_n(\phi_1^*(g)) = (\sigma'_1)^{-1}\sigma'_2$. Indeed, in virtue of the injectivity of
$\phi_1, \phi_2$ and bijectivity of $\lambda_n(g)$, there can be at most one map making 
\eqref{eq:2.1.11} commutative, and both sides of the proposed equality do.
nodes.statement_short: Uniqueness gives $\lambda_n(\phi_1^*g)=(\sigma_1')^{-1}\sigma_2'$.

nodes.name: Define $\operatorname{Res}$ on morphisms.
nodes.statement: So we define $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}$ on morphisms by sending $g$ to $\phi_1^*(g)$.
nodes.statement_short: Define $\operatorname{Res}$ on morphisms.

nodes.name: Compatibility with composition from the crossed identity.
nodes.statement:
To see that $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}$ commutes with composition of morphisms, we consider three orders
$\leq^\nu$ on $I$, $\nu=1,2,3$ with three corresponding bijections $\sigma_\nu$ and monotone maps
$\phi_\nu$. If now
$g_1=\sigma_1^{-1}\sigma_2$, $g_2=\sigma_2^{-1}\sigma_3$, then
$\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(g_1g_2)  = \phi_1^{-1}(g_1g_2)$, while
\[
\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(g_1) \circ\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(g_2) \,\,=\,\,\phi_1^*(g_1)\phi_2^*(g_2) \,\,=\,\,
\phi_1^*(g_1) \circ ((g_1^*\phi_1)^*(g_2)),
\]
which equals $\phi^*(g_1g_2)$ by the first equality in Proposition \ref{prop:skeleton}(c). We leave the
remaining verifications to the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility with composition from the crossed identity.

nodes.name: Direct construction of the restricted torsor
nodes.statement: Given a structure torsor \[ \mathcal{O}(I)\buildrel \rho\over\longrightarrow\operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n\}, I) \] for $I$, we can directly construct the ``restricted torsor" $\mathcal{O}(I')$ for $\operatorname{Res}\nolimits^I_{I'}(I, \mathcal{O}(I))$ and the canonical morphism \[ \psi=(\psi_*=u, \psi^*): (I', \mathcal{O}(I'))\to (I, \mathcal{O}(I)) \] as follows. Choose some $f\in\mathcal{O}(I)$, so that $\sigma=\lambda_{\mathcal{G}}(f)$ is a bijection defining a total order on $I$. Let $\phi: [n']\to[n]$ be the monotone map in \eqref{eq:comm-diagr-emb}. To emphasize the dependence of $\phi$ on $f$, we denote it as $\phi=f^*\psi$ (where $\psi$ stands for the morphism we are constructing). For $g,h\in\mathfrak{G}_n$ put $f.g\sim f.h$ whenever $(f^*u)^*(g)=(f^*u)^*(h)$ in $\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$. It is immediate that this is an equivalence relation, independent on the choice of $f$. We put $\mathcal{O}(I')=\mathcal{O}(I)/\sim$ and define $\psi^*: {\mathcal O}(I) \to {\mathcal O}(I')$ to be the quotient map. The composite \[ {\mathcal O}(I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n\}, I) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_ {{\bf FSet}}(\{0,1,\dots, n'\}, I) \] factors through $\psi^*$ providing a map $\rho_{I'}: {\mathcal O}(I') \to \operatorname{Isom}(\{0,1,\dots, n'\}, I)$. There exists a unique $\mathfrak{G}_{n'}$-action on ${\mathcal O}(I')$ such that, for every $f \in {\mathcal O}(I)$ and $g \in \mathfrak{G}_n$, we have \[ \psi^*(f.g) = \psi^*(f).((f^*\psi)^*g). \] It is now readily verified that this $\mathfrak{G}_m$-action on ${\mathcal O}(I)$ is simply transitive, and the maps $\psi_*=u$ and $\psi^*$ satisfy the conditions (i) and (ii) of Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}.

nodes.name: Circle
nodes.statement: By a {\em circle} we mean a topological space homeomorphic to the standard circle $S^1$.

nodes.name: Marked circle
nodes.statement:
By a {\em
marked circle} we mean a pair $(C,J)$ where $C$ is a circle and $J\subset C$ is a nonempty closed
subset homeomorphic to a finite disjoint union of copies of the interval $[0,1]$.

nodes.name: Homeomorphisms of marked circles
nodes.statement:
For two marked
circles $(C,J)$ and $(C',J')$, we denote
\[
{ \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J')) \,\,=\,\,\bigl\{ \phi\in{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(C,C') \bigl| \,\, \phi(J)\subset J'
\bigr\}. 
\]

nodes.name: Components of homeomorphism spaces are contractible
nodes.statement: Each connected component of ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J'))$ is contractible.
conclusions: Each connected component of ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J'))$ is contractible.
nodes.label: prop:homeo-contr

nodes.name: Proof of Components of homeomorphism spaces are contractible
nodes.statement: Follows from the fact that the group of orientation preserving self-homeomorphisms of an interval is contractible.
nodes.statement_short: Orientation-preserving self-homeomorphisms of an interval form a contractible group.

nodes.name: $G$-structured circle
Structured homeomorphisms of $G$-structured circles
nodes.statement:
For $G$-structured circles $(C,\rho)$ and $(C',\rho')$, we define ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,\rho), (C',\rho'))$
to be the set of pairs $(\phi, \widetilde\phi)$, where $\phi\in{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(C,C')$ and $\widetilde\phi: F\to F'$
is a ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-equivariant homeomorphism such that the diagram
\[
\xymatrix{
F\ar[d]_\rho
\ar[r]^{\widetilde\phi}& F'\ar[d]^{\rho'}
\\
{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C) \ar[r]_\phi & { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')
}
\]
is commutative.

nodes.name: Structured marked circles
nodes.statement:
We will consider circles which are both structured and marked, denoting them by $(C,J)$ where
$C=(C,\rho)$ is a $G$-structured circle. For $G$-structured marked circles $(C, J)$ and
$(C',J')$, we denote by ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,J), (C',J '))$ the closed subspace in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(C,C')$ formed by
$(\phi,\widetilde\phi)$ such that $\phi\in { \operatorname{Homeo}}((C,J), (C',J '))$.

nodes.name: Category $\mathcal{C}_G$ of structured marked circles
nodes.statement: We define the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ with objects given by $G$-structured marked circles and morphisms \[ \operatorname{Hom}_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}((C,J), (C',J')) = \pi_0\, { \operatorname{Homeo}}^G((C,J), (C',J ')). \]

nodes.name: Topological model of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$
nodes.statement: Let $p: G \to O(2)$ be a planar Lie group with corresponding crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. Then the functor \[ \lambda_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \longrightarrow {\bf FSet}, \quad (C,J)\mapsto \pi_0(J) \] canonically factors as in \[ \xymatrix{ { {\EuScript C}_G} \ar[dr]_{\lambda_{{ {\EuScript C}_G}}} \ar[rr]^{\pi}_{\simeq} & & {\mathcal G} \ar[dl]^{\lambda_{{\mathcal G}}} \\ & {\bf FSet} & } \] where ${\mathcal G}$ denotes the category of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets and $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\mathcal G}$ is an equivalence of categories. In particular, the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ is equivalent to ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: For a planar Lie group $G$, the category of $G$-structured marked circles is equivalent to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ via $(C,J)\mapsto\pi_0(J)$.
assumptions: Let $p: G \to O(2)$ be a planar Lie group with corresponding crossed simplicial group ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
conclusions: In particular, the category ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ is equivalent to ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.label: thm:CG=DG

nodes.name: Proof of Topological model of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$
nodes.statement: Let $(C,J)$ be a marked $G$-structured circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure group along $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. We claim that the association \[ (C,J) \mapsto (\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)}), \] where $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ denotes the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set constructed in Lemma \ref{lem:pi0} below, extends to an equivalence of categories $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$. Given a morphism $(\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi}): (C,J) \to (C', J')$ of marked $G$-structured circles, we have to construct a morphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ and $(\pi_0(J'),\rho_{\pi_0(J')})$. Clearly, we have an induced map $\psi: \pi_0(J) \to \pi_0(J')$ of underlying sets. We now define the pullback map $\psi^*: \pi_0(F_{J'}) \to \pi_0(F_{J})$ of structured frames. Let $f \in F_{J'}$ represent a structured frame in $\pi_0(F_{J'})$. Its image under $\rho$ defines a homeomorphism $\rho(f): { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')$ which maps $[n]$ to $J'$. We choose a point in the unique component of $C'\setminus J'$ bounded by $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$, and denote its preimage in $C$ under $\varphi$ by $p$. Note that $p$ lies in $C \setminus J$. Consider the homeomorphism $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$. Now we choose a path $\alpha: [0,1] \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ starting at $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$, ending at a homeomorphism which maps $[m]$ to $J$, such that, for all $t \in [0,1]$, $\alpha(t)(0) \ne p$. It is easy to see that the space of such paths is contractible. Since $F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ is a covering, there is a unique lift of $\alpha$ to $F$ satisfying $\alpha(0) = \widetilde{\varphi}$. We define $\psi^*(f)$ to be the connected component of $\alpha(1)$ in the space $F_J$. The pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ defines a morphism in $\mathcal{G}$ by Proposition \ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}. It straightforward to show that this construction is functorial. To see that it provides an equivalence of categories it suffices to verify the unique factorization property for the full subcategory of ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ generated by a set of standard objects $\{ (S^1, [n]) \}$ which is easily done.
nodes.statement_short: Send $(C,J)$ to the structured set $\pi_0(J)$ of Lemma 2.14; define pullback of frames by lifting paths of homeomorphisms; check unique factorization on standard objects.

nodes.name: State the functor $\pi$ to be constructed.
nodes.statement:
Let $(C,J)$ be a marked $G$-structured circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure
	group along $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. We claim that the association
	\[
		(C,J) \mapsto (\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)}),
	\] 
	where $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ denotes the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set constructed in Lemma
	\ref{lem:pi0} below, extends to an equivalence of categories $\pi: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.
nodes.statement_short: State the functor $\pi$ to be constructed.

nodes.name: A morphism induces a map of $\pi_0$.
nodes.statement:
Given a morphism $(\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi}): (C,J) \to (C', J')$ of marked
	$G$-structured circles, we have to construct a morphism of the ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets
	$(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ and $(\pi_0(J'),\rho_{\pi_0(J')})$. Clearly, we have an
	induced map $\psi: \pi_0(J) \to \pi_0(J')$ of underlying sets.
nodes.statement_short: A morphism induces a map of $\pi_0$.

nodes.name: Choose a frame and a base point avoiding $J$.
nodes.statement:
We now define the pullback
	map $\psi^*: \pi_0(F_{J'}) \to \pi_0(F_{J})$ of structured frames. Let $f \in F_{J'}$
	represent a structured frame in $\pi_0(F_{J'})$. Its image under $\rho$ defines a
	homeomorphism  $\rho(f): { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C')$ which maps $[n]$ to $J'$. We choose a point in the
	unique component of $C'\setminus J'$ bounded by $\rho(f)(n)$ and $\rho(f)(0)$, and denote
	its preimage in $C$ under $\varphi$ by $p$. Note that $p$ lies in $C \setminus J$.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a frame and a base point avoiding $J$.

nodes.name: Choose a path of homeomorphisms; the space of choices is contractible.
nodes.statement:
Consider
	the homeomorphism $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$ in ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$. Now we choose a path
	$\alpha: [0,1] \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ starting at $\varphi^{-1} \circ \rho(f)$, ending at a
	homeomorphism which maps $[m]$ to $J$, such that, for all $t \in [0,1]$, $\alpha(t)(0) \ne
	p$. It is easy to see that the space of such paths is contractible.
nodes.statement_short: Choose a path of homeomorphisms; the space of choices is contractible.

nodes.name: Lift the path and define $\psi^*(f)$.
nodes.statement:
Since $F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1,
	C)$ is a covering, there is a unique lift of $\alpha$ to $F$ satisfying $\alpha(0) =
	\widetilde{\varphi}$. We define $\psi^*(f)$ to be the connected component of $\alpha(1)$ in
	the space $F_J$.
nodes.statement_short: Lift the path and define $\psi^*(f)$.

nodes.name: Proposition 2.6 gives a morphism; functoriality.
nodes.statement:
The pair $(\psi_*, \psi^*)$ defines a morphism in $\mathcal{G}$ by Proposition
	\ref{prop:morphisms-Gc}. It straightforward to show that this construction is functorial.
nodes.statement_short: Proposition 2.6 gives a morphism; functoriality.

nodes.name: Check unique factorization on standard objects.
nodes.statement:
To see that it provides an equivalence of categories it suffices to verify the unique
	factorization property for the full subcategory of ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$ generated by a set of standard
	objects $\{ (S^1, [n]) \}$ which is easily done.
nodes.statement_short: Check unique factorization on standard objects.

nodes.name: Structured sets from $G$-structured marked circles
nodes.statement: Let $n \ge 0$ and consider the standard circle $S^1$ equipped with the standard subset $[n] \subset S^1$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity. \begin{enumerate} \item Consider the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1)$ of homeomorphisms preserving which preserve the standard subset $[n]$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity. Let $H_n$ be the pullback \[ \xymatrix{ H_n\ar[d] \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1) \ar[d]^{p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}} \\ { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \ar[r]&{ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1). } \] Then each connected component of $H_n$ is contractible and there is a canonical group isomorphism $\pi_0(H_n) \cong \mathfrak{G}_0$. \item Let $(C,J)$ be a $G$-structured marked circle with reduction $\rho: F \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ of structure group along $ p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$. Consider the subset ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J)) \subset { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, C)$ consisting of homeomorphisms which map $[n]$ into $J$ and let $\rho_J: F_J \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))$ denote the restriction of $\rho$. Then the set $\pi_0(F_J)$ is a $\pi_0(H_n)$-torsor, equipped with a natural equivariant map \[ \rho_{\pi_0(J)}: \pi_0(F_J) \to \pi_0(J) \] making $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set. \end{enumerate}
assumptions: Let $n \ge 0$ and consider the standard circle $S^1$ equipped with the standard subset
conclusions: each connected component of $H_n$ is contractible
nodes.label: lem:pi0

nodes.name: Proof of Structured sets from $G$-structured marked circles
nodes.statement: (1) As argued in Proposition \ref{prop:homeo-contr}, each component of the subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n])$ is contractible. Therefore, the map $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$ restricts to a covering $H_n \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1,[n])$ which is topologically trivial so that each connected component of $H_n$ must be contracible. We have \[ \pi_0 { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \cong D_{n+1} \cong \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_\Xi([n]) \] where $\Xi$ denotes the dihedral category of Example \ref {ex:dihedral}. The group $\pi_0(H_n)$ can be identified with the preimage $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$ under $p: G\to O(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b2), this preimage is canonically identified with $\mathfrak{G}_n$. \noindent (2) Passing to connected components, we obtain a sequence of maps \[ \pi_0(F_J) \overset{\pi_0(\rho_J)}{\longrightarrow} \pi_0({ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J))) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}([n], \pi_0(J)) \] whose composite is defined to be $\rho_{\pi_0(J)}$. It is apparent that $(\pi_0(J), \rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set.
nodes.statement_short: Covering over a space with contractible components; identify $\pi_0(H_n)$ with $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})=\mathfrak{G}_n$; compose maps on $\pi_0$.

nodes.name: Part (1): contractible components and identification with $\mathfra...
nodes.statement:
(1) As argued in Proposition \ref{prop:homeo-contr}, each component of the
 subgroup ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n])$ is contractible. Therefore, the map $p_{ \operatorname{Homeo}}$ restricts to a covering 
 $H_n \to { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1,[n])$ which is topologically trivial so that each connected component of $H_n$
 must be contracible. We have
 \[
	 \pi_0 { \operatorname{Homeo}}(S^1, [n]) \cong D_{n+1} \cong \operatorname{Aut}\nolimits_\Xi([n])
 \]
 where $\Xi$ denotes the dihedral category of Example \ref {ex:dihedral}. The group $\pi_0(H_n)$ can
 be identified with the preimage $p^{-1}(D_{n+1})$ under $p: G\to O(2)$. By Theorem \ref{thm:crossed-groups}(b2), 
 this preimage is canonically identified with $\mathfrak{G}_n$.
nodes.statement_short: Part (1): contractible components and identification with $\mathfrak{G}_n$.

nodes.name: Part (2): compose maps on connected components.
nodes.statement:
(2) Passing to connected components, we obtain a sequence of maps
	\[
			\pi_0(F_J) \overset{\pi_0(\rho_J)}{\longrightarrow} \pi_0({ \operatorname{Homeo}}( (S^1, [n]), (C, J)))
			\longrightarrow \operatorname{Isom}_{{\bf FSet}}([n],
			\pi_0(J))
	\]
	whose composite is defined to be $\rho_{\pi_0(J)}$. It is apparent that $(\pi_0(J),
	\rho_{\pi_0(J)})$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set.
nodes.statement_short: Part (2): compose maps on connected components.

nodes.name: Structured circles induce structured orders
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be a $G$-structured circle. Then, for any nonempty finite subset $I\subset C$, both $I$ and $\pi_0(C-I)$ acquire canonical ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structures. These structures are natural with respect to homeomorphisms of $G$-structured circles.
assumptions: Let $C$ be a $G$-structured circle.
nodes.label: cor:structured-circle-orders

nodes.name: $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$ acts on geometric realization
nodes.statement: Let $R:{\mathcal Set}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}\to{\mathcal Top}$ be the geometric realization functor: $R(X)=|i^*X|$, where $i: \Delta\to{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is the embedding. The group ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ acts on $R$ by natural isomoprhisms. In particular, it acts on each $|i^*X|$ be homeomorphisms.
nodes.statement_short: The planar homeomorphism group acts by natural isomorphisms on the geometric realization functor of $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-sets.
conclusions: The group ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ acts on $R$ by natural isomoprhisms.

nodes.name: $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)=\operatorname{Aut}(R)$
nodes.statement:
It seems plausible that the group ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$ is in fact identified with $\operatorname{Aut}\nolimits(R)$
 which would provide its natural construction in terms of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$.

nodes.name: Proof of $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$ acts on geometric realization
nodes.statement: The argument is similar to that of \cite{drinfeld:cyclic}. That is, let $\bf\Delta$ be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, and ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta}\to \mathcal{G}$ be the functor of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure, extending $i$ (Example \ref{ex:DG-closure}). A simplicial set $Y$ can be seen as a contravariant functor $Y: {\bf\Delta}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and, as pointed out in Formula (1.1) of \cite {drinfeld:cyclic}, \[ |Y|\,\,=\,\,\varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, Y\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr), \] where $F$ runs over finite subsets of $[0,1]$, and $\pi_0([0,1]-F)$ is equipped by the total order induced by that on $[0,1]$. Now, if $X$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set, we can view $X$ as a contravariant functor $\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and identify \[ \begin{gathered} |i^*X| \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, ({\bf i}^*X)\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0([0,1]-F))\bigr) \,\,= \\ =\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{1\in F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr) \,\,=\,\, \,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr). \end{gathered} \] Here we view $S^1$ as obtained from $[0,1]$ by identifying $0$ and $1$ into one point $1\in S^1$ and as equipped with the standard ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure. Each set $\pi_0(S^1-F)$ is then equipped with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}. Now, the last colimit is manifestly acted upon by ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Following Drinfeld, write realization as a colimit over finite subsets of the circle, on which $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$ manifestly acts.

nodes.name: Follow Drinfeld; use the $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-closure functor.
nodes.statement:
The argument is similar to that of \cite{drinfeld:cyclic}. 
 That is, let $\bf\Delta$ be the category of all nonempty finite ordinals, and ${\bf i}: {\bf\Delta}\to \mathcal{G}$
 be the functor of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-closure, extending $i$ (Example \ref{ex:DG-closure}).
nodes.statement_short: Follow Drinfeld; use the $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-closure functor.

nodes.name: Drinfeld's colimit formula for realization.
nodes.statement:
A simplicial set $Y$ can
 be seen as a contravariant functor $Y: {\bf\Delta}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and, as pointed out in Formula (1.1) of
 \cite {drinfeld:cyclic},
 \[
 |Y|\,\,=\,\,\varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, Y\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr), 
 \]
 where $F$ runs over finite subsets of $[0,1]$, and $\pi_0([0,1]-F)$ is equipped by the total order
 induced by that on $[0,1]$.
nodes.statement_short: Drinfeld's colimit formula for realization.

nodes.name: Rewrite $|i^*X|$ as a colimit over finite subsets of $S^1$.
nodes.statement:
Now, if $X$ is a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set, we can view $X$ as a contravariant functor $\mathcal{G}\to{\mathcal Set}$ and identify
 \[
 \begin{gathered}
 |i^*X| \,\,=\,\, \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, ({\bf i}^*X)\bigl( \pi_0([0,1]-F)\bigr) \,\,=\,\,
 \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset [0,1]} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0([0,1]-F))\bigr) \,\,= \\
=\,\,   \varinjlim\limits_{1\in F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr) \,\,=\,\,
  \,\,  \varinjlim\limits_{F\subset S^1} \, X\bigl({\bf i} ( \pi_0(S^1-F))\bigr).
  \end{gathered}
 \]
 Here we view $S^1$ as obtained from $[0,1]$ by identifying $0$ and $1$ into one point $1\in S^1$ and as equipped
 with the standard ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$-structure. Each set $\pi_0(S^1-F)$ is then equipped with a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structure
 by Corollary \ref{cor:structured-circle-orders}.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite $|i^*X|$ as a colimit over finite subsets of $S^1$.

nodes.name: The colimit is acted on by $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$.
nodes.statement:
Now, the last colimit is manifestly acted upon by
 ${ \operatorname{Homeo}}^G(S^1)$. \qed
nodes.statement_short: The colimit is acted on by $\operatorname{Homeo}^G(S^1)$.

nodes.name: Self-duality of planar crossed simplicial groups
nodes.statement: Any planar crossed simplicial group is self-dual.
conclusions: Any planar crossed simplicial group is self-dual.
nodes.label: cor:duality

nodes.name: Proof of Self-duality of planar crossed simplicial groups
nodes.statement: We define the functor $(-)^{\vee}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to { {\EuScript C}_G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ by putting \[ (C,J)^{\vee} := (C, \overline{C \setminus J}), \quad (\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi})^{\vee} := (\varphi^{-1}, \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1}) \] on objects and morphisms, respectively. Since the square of this functor equals the identity functor, it must be an equivalence. Further, since ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is equivalent to ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$, we conclude that there exists a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \overset{\simeq}{\to} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\operatorname{op}}$ with $[n]^\vee=[n]$. The choice of values for this functor on morphisms, however, is not canonical.
nodes.statement_short: Interstice duality $(C,J)\mapsto(C,\overline{C\setminus J})$ is an involutive equivalence of $\mathcal{C}_G$, transported to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$.

nodes.name: Define the interstice functor.
nodes.statement:
We define the  functor $(-)^{\vee}: { {\EuScript C}_G} \to
	{ {\EuScript C}_G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$  by putting
		\[
		(C,J)^{\vee} := (C, \overline{C \setminus J}), \quad 
 (\varphi, \widetilde{\varphi})^{\vee} := (\varphi^{-1}, \widetilde{\varphi}^{-1})
	\]
	on objects and morphisms, respectively.
nodes.statement_short: Define the interstice functor.

nodes.name: It squares to the identity, hence an equivalence.
nodes.statement: Since the square of this functor equals the identity functor, it must be an equivalence.
nodes.statement_short: It squares to the identity, hence an equivalence.

nodes.name: Transport to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ via Theorem 2.13.
nodes.statement:
Further, since ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ is equivalent to ${ {\EuScript C}_G}$, we conclude that there exists a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}:
	{\Delta \mathfrak{G}} \overset{\simeq}{\to} {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\operatorname{op}}$ with $[n]^\vee=[n]$. The choice of values for this functor on morphisms, however, is
	not canonical.
nodes.statement_short: Transport to $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$ via Theorem 2.13.

nodes.name: Interstices
nodes.statement:
The connected components of $\overline{C \setminus J}$ can be regarded as ``interstices" positioned
between adjacent connected components of $J$.

nodes.name: Linear growth of $\mathfrak{G}_n$
nodes.statement: After choosing a duality functor $(-)^\vee_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$, we obtain identifications of sets \[ \begin{gathered} \mathfrak{G}_n \,\, \buildrel \operatorname{C.F.} \over = \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([n], [0]) \,\,\simeq \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0]^\vee, [n]^\vee)\,\,\simeq \\ \simeq \,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n]) \,\, \buildrel \operatorname{C.F.} \over = \,\, \mathfrak{G}_0 \times \operatorname{Hom}_\Delta([0], [n]), \end{gathered} \] where ``C.F." stands for the canonical factorization of morphisms in a crossed simplicial group. These identifications can be interpreted by saying that $\mathfrak{G}_n$ ``grows linearly with $n$" (with ``coefficient of proportionality" being $\mathfrak{G}_0$). Cf. the discussion of three growth types of crossed simplicial groups in \S \ref{sub:weyl}. We further deduce that the $\mathfrak{G}_n$-action on $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}([0], [n])$ is simply transitive.
nodes.label: rems:duality

nodes.name: Combinatorial duality
nodes.statement: One can also give a purely combinatorial description of duality in terms of the category $\mathcal{G}$ of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured sets. Note that for any object $(I, \mathcal{O}(I))\in{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$ we have canonical identifications \[ I \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}}([0], I)/\mathfrak{G}_0, \quad \mathcal{O}(I) \,\,=\,\, \operatorname{Hom}_{\mathcal{G}}(I, [0]). \] The dual of $(I, {\mathcal O}(I))$ is the pair \[ (I^{\vee}, {\mathcal O}(I^{\vee})) := (\operatorname{Hom}_{{\mathcal G}}(I, [0])/\mathfrak{G}_0, \operatorname{Hom}_{{\mathcal G}}([0],I)) \] which can be made into a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured set so that $I \mapsto I^{\vee}$ defines an equivalence ${\mathcal G} \to {\mathcal G}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$.

nodes.name: Total cyclic order
nodes.statement: A {\em (total) cyclic order} on a finite set $J$ of cardinality $n$ is the choice of a simply transitive action of the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$. Note that a cyclic order on the set $J$ is uniquely determined by specifying for every element $j$ its {\em successor} $j + 1$.
nodes.genus: choice of a simply transitive action of the group $\mathbb{Z}/n\mathbb{Z}$
nodes.label: def:totalcyclic

nodes.name: Examples of cyclic orders; cyclic closure and lexicographic order
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Any set of cardinality $\le 2$ has a unique cyclic order. A cyclic order on a set $J$ of cardinality $3$ is the same as an orientation of the triangle $|\Delta^J|$. \item Every subset of a cyclically ordered set $J$ has a canonical cyclic order. \item Any finite linearly ordered set $J$ carries a canonical cyclic order where the successor of each nonmaximal element of $J$ is its successor with respect to the linear order and the minimal element is the successor of the maximal element. We say that this cyclic order is the {\em cyclic closure} of the linear order on $J$. \item More generally, given a cyclically ordered finite set $K$ and a map of finite sets $f: J \to K$ where each fiber of $f$ is equipped with a linear order, we can define the {\em lexicographic} cyclic order on $J$ as follows. First note, that the set of fibers of $f$ is canonically identified with $K$ and hence carries a cyclic order. Therefore, every fiber has a successor fiber. Now the cyclic order on $J$ is given as follows: For every element $j$ which is nonmaximal in its fiber, we define the successor $j +1$ to be the successor with respect to the specified linear order of the fiber. If $j$ is maximal in its fiber, we define its successor to be the minimal element of the successor fiber. Here the convention is to skip all empty fibers. The previous example is then given by the case when $K$ is a point, equipped with its unique cyclic order. \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Large cyclic category
nodes.statement: A morphism $f: J \to K$ of finite cyclically ordered sets is a map $f: J \to K$ of underlying sets equipped with the choice of a linear order on every fiber such that the cyclic order on $J$ is the induced lexicographic order. The resulting category ${\bf \Lambda}$ given by finite nonempty cyclically ordered sets and their morphisms is called the {\em large cyclic category.}
definiendum: morphism of finite cyclically ordered sets

nodes.name: Combinatorial description of Connes' category
nodes.statement: (a) Restricting to the standard cyclic ordinals $\langle n \rangle$, this gives a purely combinatorial description of morphisms in Connes' category $\Lambda$. (b) We have a natural faithful embedding ${\bf \Delta} \subset {\bf \Lambda}$ given by associating to a linearly ordered set $J$ its cyclic closure. This extends the embedding $\Delta\subset\Lambda$.

nodes.name: Partial cyclic order
nodes.label: def:cyclic-order

nodes.name: Examples of partial cyclic orders
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item Let $C$ be a circle. Then $C^3_\neq = C^3-\bigcup_{i\neq j} \{x_i=x_j\}$ has two connected components which are in bijection with orientations of $C$. The ``anti-clockwise" component corrresponding to a choice of orientation contains triples $(x_1, x_2, x_3)$ with $x_i$ following very closely each other in the orientation direction. The closure $\lambda$ of this component is a total cyclic order on $C$. In particular, the standard oriented circle $S^1 = \{|z|=1\}\subset\mathbb{C}$ has a canonical cyclic order. This implies that a total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ can be defined as an homeomorphism class of embeddings of $J$ into oriented circles. That is, two such embeddings $u: J\to C$ and $u':J\to C'$ are identified iff there is an orientation preserving homeomorphism $\phi: C\to C'$ such that $\phi u=u'$. It is now easy to verify that a total cyclic order on a finite set as defined in Definition \ref{def:cyclic-order} is the same as a total cyclic order in the sense of Definition \ref{def:totalcyclic}. \item Let $\leq$ be a partial linear order on $S$. Its {\em cyclic closure} is the ternary relation $\lambda=\lambda_\leq\subset S^3$ obtained as the closure of the set $\{x_1\leq x_2\leq x_3\}$ under the action of $\mathbb{Z}/3$ by cyclic rotations. It is straightforward to see that $\lambda$ is a partial cyclic order, total if $\leq$ is a total linear order, cf. \cite[Th. 3.5]{novak}. This implies that total cyclic order on a finite set $J$ with $|J|=n$ is the same as a class of bijections $J\to \{1, 2, ..., n\}$ under the action of $\mathbb{Z}/n$, each bijection (i.e., a total order) giving a cyclic order by cyclic closure. \item Every set $J$ has the {\em discrete partial cyclic order} consisting only of triples $(a,a,a)$, $a\in J$. If $|J|=1$, this is the only partial cyclic order on $J$. If $|J|=2$, then $J$ has two partial cyclic orders: one discrete and the other is the total cyclic order, formed by all triples $(a,b,c)\in J^3$. Note that Nov\'ak's setting \cite{novak} allows only one partial cyclic order on a 2-element set, the discrete one. \item Generalizing (1), one can see that the set of points of any ``abstract circle" in the sense of Moerdijk \cite{moerdijk} has a total cyclic order. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: ex:cyclic-orders

nodes.name: Cyclic order on flag varieties (Fock-Goncharov)
nodes.statement: The real projective line $\mathbb{R} P^1$, being a circle, has a cyclic order. Such an order is determined by a choice of orientation of $\mathbb{R}^2$. More generally, let $F_n=\operatorname{Flag}(1,2,...,n; \mathbb{R}^n)$ be the space of complete flags in $\mathbb{R}^n$. For example, $F_2=\mathbb{R} P^1$. One of the main results of \cite{fock-goncharov} (theory of positive configurations of flags) says, in our terminology, that $F_n$ has a natural partial cyclic order $\lambda$, determined by a choice of orientation of $\mathbb{R}^n$. Explicitly, a closed smooth curve $C\subset \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ is called {\em convex}, if every hyperplane intersects $C$ in at most $n-1$ points. In particular, such $C$ does not lie in a hyperplane. Taking the osculating flags to $C$ at all its points, we obtain an embedding $\gamma_C: C\to F_n$. The 2-element set of orientations of any convex curve $C\subset \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ is canonically identified with the 2-element set of orientations of $\mathbb{R}^n$, by a version of the Frenet frame construction (this is the old-fashioned definition of the orientation of the space in terms of ``left and right screws"). Thus choosing an orientation of $\mathbb{R}^n$, we equip any convex $C$ with a total cyclic order $\lambda_C$. We then say that $({\bf f}_1, {\bf f}_2, {\bf f}_3)\in F_n^3$ lies in $\lambda$, if there is a convex curve $C\in \mathbb{R} P^{n-1}$ and three points $(t_1, t_2, t_3)\in\lambda_C$ such that ${\bf f}_i=\gamma_C(t_i)$. See {\em loc. cit.} for more details as well as a generalization to the complete flag variety of any split simple algebraic group over $\mathbb{R}$.

nodes.name: Lexicographic cyclic order
nodes.statement:
Let $f: I	o J$ be a map of sets. Suppose that $J$ is equipped with a partial cyclic order $\lambda_J$, and each fiber $f^{-1}(j)$ is equipped with a partial linear order $\leq_j$. In this setting we construct a partial cyclic order $\lambda=\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ on $I$, called the {\em lexicographic cyclic order} as follows. We say that $(a,b,c)\in\lambda_I$ if $(f(a), f(b), f(c))\in\lambda_J$ and either  egin{enumerate}[labelindent=1cm] \item[(i)] all three elements $f(a), f(b), f(c)$ are distinct, or: \item[(ii)] $f(a)=f(b)
eq f(c)$ and $a\leq_{f(a)} b$, or: \item[(ii')] $f(a)=f(c)
eq f(b)$ and $c\leq_{f(c)} a$, or: \item[(ii'')] $f(a)
eq f(b)=f(c)$ and $b\leq_{f(b)} c$, or: \item[(iii)] $f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$ and either  egin{enumerate} \item $a\leq_j b\leq_j c$, or \item $b\leq_j c\leq_j a$, or \item $c\leq_j a\leq_j b$, \,\, $j=f(a)=f(b)=f(c)$. \end{enumerate} \end{enumerate} If $\lambda_J$ is a total cyclic order, and each $\leq_i$ is a total linear order, then $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))$ is a total cyclic order.
nodes.label: defi:lexico

nodes.name: Morphisms of partially cyclically ordered sets
nodes.statement: Let $(I,\lambda_I)$ and $(J, \lambda_J)$ be partially cyclically ordered sets. \begin{enumerate}[label=(\alph*),itemsep=0cm,topsep=1ex] \item Assume that $\lambda_I$ is a total cyclic order. Then we define a {\em morphism} $F: I\to J$ to be a datum consisting of a map $f: I\to J$ and a total linear order $\leq_j$ on each $f^{-1}(j)$ such that $\operatorname{Lex}(f, (\leq_j))=\lambda_I$. \item In general, a morphism $F: I\to J$ is a compatible system of morphisms $I'\to J$ given for all totally cyclically ordered subsets $I'\subset I$ (with respect to the induced cyclic order). \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:morphisms-cyclic-orders

nodes.name: Injective morphisms
nodes.statement:
If $f$ is injective, then $F$ is
determined by $f$. We call such morphisms {\em injective}.

nodes.name: Category $\mathbf{\Lambda}_{par}$
nodes.statement:
The collection of partially cyclically ordered sets with morphisms as defined above forms a category
${\mathbf \Lambda}_{\operatorname{par}}$ which contains the categories $\Lambda$ and ${\bf \Lambda}$ as full
subcategories.

nodes.name: Cyclic dual $J^\vee$
nodes.statement:
Given a cyclically
ordered set $J$ of cardinality $n \ge 1$,  the set $J^{\vee} := \operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(J, \langle 0\rangle)$
 is, by definition, in canonical bijection with the
set of {\em linear refinements} of the cyclic order on $J$, i.e., linear orders whose cyclic closure recovers 
the cyclic order on $J$. Further, the action of $\mathbb{Z}/n$ on $J$ induces a $\mathbb{Z}/n$-action on
$J^{\vee}$ which is simply transitive.

nodes.name: Interstices of a subset of the circle
nodes.statement: Let $J \subset S^1$ be a subset of the standard circle. Providing $J$ with the counter-clockwise cyclic order induced from $S^1$, we may identify the set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\Lambda}(J, \langle 0\rangle)$ with the set of homotopy classes of monotone maps $f: S^1 \to S^1$ of degree $1$ taking the subset $J$ to $1 \in S^1$. Let us refer to the arcs on $S^1$ which connect an element of $J$ to its successor as {\em interstices of $J$}. The map $f$ is uniquely determined by specifying which interstice of $J$ maps to a nontrivial loop in $S^1$. Therefore, $J^{\vee}$ is canonically identified with the set of interstices of $J \subset S^1$. For an abstract cyclically ordered set, the set $J^{\vee}$ should be regarded as an intrinsic construction of the set of interstices with its cyclic order, without any reference to an embedding into the circle. The role of $J^\vee$ as a dual object was emphasized by Drinfeld \cite{drinfeld:cyclic} whose result can be formulated as follows.

nodes.name: Cyclic interstice duality
nodes.statement: The cyclic interstice construction $J \mapsto J^{\vee}$ extends to a functor \[ {\bf \Lambda}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\bf \Lambda} \] which is an equivalence of categories.
conclusions: which is an equivalence of categories.
nodes.label: prop:cyclic-interstice

nodes.name: Proof of Cyclic interstice duality
nodes.statement: Although this is a particular case of the general duality for planar crossed simplicial groups, let us provide a self-contained proof for convenience of the reader. Given a morphism of cyclically ordered sets $f: J \to K$, we obtain a map of sets of linear refinements $f^{\vee}: K^{\vee} \to J^{\vee}$. To lift this map to a morphism of cyclically ordered sets, we have to additionally provide a linear order on each fiber of $f^{\vee}$. Consider linear orders $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in K^{\vee}$ which map to the same linear order $\lambda \in J^{\vee}$. Let $j_{\max}$ be the maximum of $(J, \lambda)$. We say $\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2$ if \[ \big|\{k \in K\; |\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_1} k\}\big| \le \big|\{k \in K \;|\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_2} k\}\big|. \] This construction provides linear orders on the fibers of $f^{\vee}$ which are compatible with the cyclic order on $K^{\vee}$. The equivalence of categories can be verified by noting that the double dual $(J^{\vee})^{\vee}$ can be canonically and functorially identified with $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Order the fibers of $f^\vee$ by counting elements after $f(j_{\max})$; equivalence since the double dual is $J$.

nodes.name: Self-contained proof instead of the general duality.
nodes.statement:
Although this is a particular case of the general duality for planar crossed
	simplicial groups, let us provide a self-contained proof for convenience of the reader.
nodes.statement_short: Self-contained proof instead of the general duality.

nodes.name: $f$ induces $f^\vee$ on linear refinements; need fiber orders.
nodes.statement:
Given a morphism of cyclically ordered sets $f: J \to K$, we obtain a map of sets of linear
	refinements $f^{\vee}: K^{\vee} \to J^{\vee}$. To lift this map to a morphism of cyclically ordered sets,
	we have to additionally provide a linear order on each fiber of $f^{\vee}$.
nodes.statement_short: $f$ induces $f^\vee$ on linear refinements; need fiber orders.

nodes.name: Define the order on fibers of $f^\vee$.
nodes.statement:
Consider linear
	orders $\lambda_1, \lambda_2 \in K^{\vee}$ which map to the same linear order $\lambda \in
	J^{\vee}$. Let $j_{\max}$ be the maximum of $(J, \lambda)$. We say $\lambda_1 \le \lambda_2$ if
	\[
		\big|\{k \in K\; |\; f(j_{\max}) \le_{\lambda_1} k\}\big| \le \big|\{k \in K \;|\; f(j_{\max})
		\le_{\lambda_2} k\}\big|.
	\]
nodes.statement_short: Define the order on fibers of $f^\vee$.

nodes.name: Compatibility with the cyclic order on $K^\vee$.
nodes.statement:
This construction provides linear orders on the fibers of $f^{\vee}$
	which are compatible with the cyclic order on $K^{\vee}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compatibility with the cyclic order on $K^\vee$.

nodes.name: Double dual identifies with $J$.
nodes.statement:
The equivalence of categories can
	be verified by noting that the double dual $(J^{\vee})^{\vee}$ can be canonically and
	functorially identified with $J$.
nodes.statement_short: Double dual identifies with $J$.

nodes.name: Opposite cyclic order
nodes.statement:
Given a finite set $J$ with cyclic order $\lambda$, we can define the {\em opposite} cyclic order
$\lambda^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ on $J$ by declaring the successor $j+1$ of an element $j$ to be the predecessor 
$j-1$ of $j$ with respect to $\lambda$. The association $(J,\lambda) \mapsto (J, \lambda^{{\operatorname{op}}})$ extends to a self-equivalence of the
category $\bf \Lambda$ where the opposite $f^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ of a morphism $f: J \to K$ is defined to be the
same map on underlying sets equipped with the opposite linear order on each fiber.

nodes.name: Dihedral order
nodes.statement: A {\em dihedral order} on a finite set $J$ of cardinality $\ge 3$ is defined to be the choice of a set $o(J) = \{\lambda_0,\lambda_1\}$ of opposite cyclic orders on $J$. A dihedral order on a set $J$ of cardinality $\le 2$ is defined to be the choice of an arbitrary two-element set $o(J)$. Given a dihedrally ordered set $(J, o(J))$, we refer to the two-element set $o(J)$ as the {\em orientation torsor} of $J$.

nodes.name: Large dihedral category
nodes.statement:
A morphism $J \to K$ of dihedrally ordered sets is defined to be a
bijection $f: o(J) \to o(K)$ and an unordered pair $\{f_0:(J,\lambda_0) \to  (K, f(\lambda_0)),f_1: (J,
\lambda_1) \to (K, f(\lambda_1))\}$ of opposite morphisms of cyclic ordinals. Here, we agree by
convention that for a dihedrally ordered set $J$ of cardinality $\le 2$, both elements of the
orientation torsor $o(J)$ induce the unique cyclic order on $J$. With this notion of morphism, the
set of finite nonempty dihedrally ordered sets organizes into a category ${\bf \Xi}$ which we call the {\em large
dihedral category}.

nodes.name: Virtual orientation torsor
nodes.statement: (a) The reason for the introduction of a ``virtual'' orientation torsor for sets of cardinality $\le 2$ should now be clear. For example, with this convention, the automorphism groups of the standard dihedrally ordered sets $\{0\}$ and $\{0,1\}$ are $D_1 = \mathbb{Z}/2$ and $D_2 = \mathbb{Z}/2 \times \mathbb{Z}/2$, respectively. The nontrivial automorphism given by interchanging the elements of the virtual orientation torsor acts trivially on the underlying sets. \vskip .2cm (b) The automorphism of $\bf \Lambda$ given by passing to the opposite cyclic order can be regarded as an action of the (discrete $2$-) group $\mathbb{Z}/2$ on $\bf \Lambda$. Our approach amounts to defining $\bf\Xi$ as the quotient of $\bf\Lambda$ by this action.

nodes.name: Examples of dihedral orders; dihedral closure
nodes.label: exa:dihedral

nodes.name: Dihedral orders and real points of $\overline M_{0,J}$
nodes.statement: A more algebro-geometric version of Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \ref{exa:item2} can be obtained as follows. Let $J$ be a finite set with $\geq 3$ elements, and $\overline M_{0,J}$ be the moduli space of stable $J$-pointed curves of genus 0. This is a smooth projective variety over $\mathbb{Q}$ of dimension $|J|-3$ whose open part is the quotient \[ M_{0,J} = \bigl( (\mathbb{P}^1)^J \setminus (\text{diagonals} )\bigr) \bigl/ PGL_2, \] see, e.g., \cite{kapranov-veronese} for more details. Now note that connected components of the real locus $M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ are in bijection with dihedral orders on $J$. Indeed, $\mathbb{R} P^1= \mathbb{P}^1(\mathbb{R})$ is topologically a circle, and action of $PGL_2(\mathbb{R})$ on it contains transformations both preserving and reversing the orientation of this circle, so a comparison as in Example \ref{exa:dihedral} \eqref{exa:item2} is immediate. It was proved in \cite{kapranov-permuto} that the closure in $\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ of each component of $M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$, is identified with the Stasheff polytope $K_{|J|-1}$. Thus $\overline M_{0,J}(\mathbb{R})$ can be obtained by gluing as many Stasheff polytopes as there are dihedral orders on $J$.

nodes.name: Tuples of distinct elements and the relation $\gamma$
nodes.statement:
For any $n\geq 1$ let
\[
	J^n_\neq = J^n \setminus \bigcup_{i\neq j} \{x_i=x_j\}
\]
be the set of $n$-tuples of distinct elements of $J$, and let $\gamma \subset J^4_\neq$
consist of $4$-tuples $(a,b,c,d)$ such that dihedral order on $\{a,b,c,d\}$ induced from the
embedding into $J$ coincides with the dihedral closure of the linear order $(a,b,c,d)$.

nodes.name: Face tuples $\partial_i\mathbf{x}$
nodes.statement:
For any ${\bf x}= (x_0, \dots , x_4)\in J^5_\neq$ let
\[
	\partial_i {\bf x} = (x_0, \dots, \widehat x_i, \dots, x_4), \quad i=0, \dots, 4, 
\]
be the tuple obtained by removing the $i$th element.

nodes.name: The pentagon property for dihedral orders
nodes.statement: Let $J$ be a finite dihedrally ordered set, $|J|\geq 5$, and $\gamma\subset J^4_\neq$ defined as above. For any ${\bf x}=(x_0, \dots, x_4) \in J^5_\neq$ the following are equivalent: \begin{enumerate} \item[(i)] All $\partial_i {\bf x}$, $i=0, \dots, 4$, belong to $\gamma$. In order words, the total order on $\{x_0, \dots, x_4\}$ is compatible with the induced cyclic order. \item[(ii)] $\partial_1{\bf x}$ and $\partial_3 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$. \item[(iii)] $\partial_0{\bf x}$, $\partial_2{\bf x}$ and $\partial_4 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.statement_short: Five distinct points are in dihedral position iff two (resp. three) of their 4-element faces are.
assumptions: Let $J$ be a finite dihedrally ordered set, $|J|\geq 5$
defined as above.
equivalent_conditions: $\partial_0{\bf x}$, $\partial_2{\bf x}$ and $\partial_4 {\bf x}$ belong to $\gamma$.

nodes.name: Proof of The pentagon property for dihedral orders
nodes.statement: Clearly, (i) implies (ii) and (iii). Let us prove that (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i). Let $J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order. Since $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral order. In other words, their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$ into the following (unoriented) arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and $A(x_4, x_0)$. Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$. With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$ must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. Now, the assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. The proof that (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is similar. In fact, the conditions $\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$ and $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ already imply (i), the situation differing from (ii) by a cyclic rotation.
nodes.statement_short: Embed $J$ in a circle; $\partial_1\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ fixes four arcs and $\partial_3\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ forces $x_1$ into the right arc.

nodes.name: (ii) implies (i)
nodes.statement:
Clearly, (i) implies (ii) and (iii). Let us prove that (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).  Let
	$J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order.   Since
	$\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral
	order.  In other words,  their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$
	into the following  (unoriented)  arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and
	$A(x_4, x_0)$.  Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain
	any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$.  With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$
	must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely  when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$. Now, the
	assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses
	the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) gives (ii),(iii); prove (ii)$\Rightarrow$(i).

nodes.name: $\partial_1\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ cuts the circle into four arcs.
nodes.statement:
Let
	$J\hookrightarrow C$ be an embedding into a circle defining the dihedral order.   Since
	$\partial_1{\bf x}\in\gamma$, we have that $x_0, x_2, x_3, x_4$ are in the right dihedral
	order.  In other words,  their embedding into a circle $C$ is such that they subdivide $C$
	into the following  (unoriented)  arcs: $A(x_0, x_2)$, $A(x_2, x_3)$, $A(x_3, x_4)$ and
	$A(x_4, x_0)$.  Here $A(x_p, x_q)$ denotes the arc joining $x_p, x_q$ which does not contain
	any other $x_j, j\in \{0,2,3,4\}$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial_1\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ cuts the circle into four arcs.

nodes.name: (i) holds iff $x_1\in A(x_0,x_2)$.
nodes.statement:
With respect to this embedding into $C$, the point $x_1$
	must lie on one of these arcs, and (i) holds precisely  when $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: (i) holds iff $x_1\in A(x_0,x_2)$.

nodes.name: $\partial_3\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ puts $x_1$ in $A(x_0,x_2)$.
nodes.statement:
Now, the
	assumption that $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ means that the diagonal $[x_0, x_2]$ crosses
	the diagonal $[x_1, x_4]$ which means that $x_1\in A(x_0, x_2)$.
nodes.statement_short: $\partial_3\mathbf{x}\in\gamma$ puts $x_1$ in $A(x_0,x_2)$.

nodes.name: (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is the same up to rotation.
nodes.statement:
The proof that (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is similar. In fact, the conditions $\partial_1{\bf
	 x}\in\gamma$ and $\partial_3{\bf x}\in\gamma$ already imply (i), the situation differing from (ii)
	 by a cyclic rotation.
nodes.statement_short: (iii)$\Rightarrow$(i) is the same up to rotation.

nodes.name: Dihedral dual $J^\vee$
nodes.statement:
Given any finite nonempty dihedrally ordered set $J$, consider the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}} :=
\operatorname{Hom}_{{\bf \Xi}}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$. We can identify the set $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ with the set of pairs
$(\lambda, o)$ where $o \in O(J)$ is an orientation and $\lambda$ is a linear refinement of the
cyclic order on $J$ corresponding to $o$. In particular, $\widetilde{J^{\vee}}$ admits a natural
involution given by $(\lambda,o) \mapsto (\lambda^{{\operatorname{op}}}, o^{{\operatorname{op}}})$. We define $J^{\vee}$ to be the
orbit set under this involution. We can interpret $O(J)$ as an orientation torsor for $J^{\vee}$
which determines opposite cyclic orders on $J^{\vee}$. Hence $J^{\vee}$ admits a canonical dihedral
order.

nodes.name: Oriented and unoriented interstices
nodes.statement: Let $J \subset S^1$ be a subset of the standard circle considered without chosen orientation. Then $J$ inherits a natural dihedral order and the morphism set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ can be identified with homotopy classes of monotone homotopy equivalences $f:S^1 \to S^1$ which map the subset $J$ to the point $1 \in S^1$ where we orient the target circle counterclockwise. This map $f$ is uniquely determined by the choice of an orientation and the choice of an interstice which maps to a nontrivial loop in $S^1$. Therefore, $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})$ is in natural bijection with the set of {\em oriented interstices} of $J \subset S^1$. The quotient set $\operatorname{Hom}_{\bf \Xi}(J, \overline {\langle 0\rangle})/(\mathbb{Z}/2)$ is then identified with the set of {\em unoriented interstices}. The two possible choice of coherent orientations of all interstices correspond to the elements of the orientation torsor.

nodes.name: Dihedral interstice duality
nodes.statement: The dihedral interstice construction $J \mapsto J^{\vee}$ extends to a functor \[ {\bf \Xi}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \longrightarrow {\bf \Xi} \] which is an equivalence of categories. \qed
conclusions: which is an equivalence of categories.
nodes.label: prop:dihedral-interstice

nodes.name: Paracyclic order
nodes.statement: A {\em paracyclic order} on a finite nonempty set $J$ consists of \begin{enumerate} \item a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor $\widetilde{J}$, \item a surjection $\pi: \widetilde{J} \to J$ which exhibits $J$ as the orbit set of the bijection \[T:\; \widetilde{J} \to \widetilde{J},\quad \widetilde{j} \mapsto \widetilde{j} + |J|.\] \end{enumerate}

nodes.name: Paracyclic orders from base points on a circle
nodes.statement: Let $C$ be an oriented circle. A choice of a base point $c\in C$ defines a canonical paracyclic order on any finite nonempty $J\subset C$. More precisely, the choice of $c$ produces a canonical universal covering $\pi: \widetilde C_c\to C$, with $\widetilde C_c$ being homeomorphic to $\mathbb{R}$ and oriented, and so equipped with a canonical total order. The discrete subset $\widetilde j=\pi^{-1}(J)$ has a natural successor operation induced by the order on $\widetilde C_c$, which makes it into a $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor. The generator of the group $\mathbb{Z}$ of deck transformations on $\widetilde C_c$ corresponds to the shift by $|J|$ in this torsor structure.
nodes.label: exa:paracyclic-exp

nodes.name: Large paracyclic category
nodes.statement:
A morphism $(J, \widetilde{J}) \to (K, \widetilde{K})$ of paracyclically ordered sets is given by a
commutative diagram 
\[
	\xymatrix{
		\widetilde{J} \ar[d]_{\pi_J} \ar[r]^{\widetilde{f}} & \ar[d]^{\pi_K} \widetilde{K}\\
		J \ar[r]^f &  K
	}
\]
such that $\widetilde{f}$ is monotone with respect to the linear orders on $\widetilde{J}$ and $\widetilde{K}$
induced from the $\mathbb{Z}$-torsor structures. 
The resulting category of finite nonempty paracyclically ordered
sets is called the {\em large paracyclic category} denoted by ${\bf \Lambda_{\infty}}$.

nodes.name: $\mathbb{Z}$-ordered set
nodes.statement:
Following \cite[\S 3.1]{HSS1}, call a $\mathbb{Z}$-{\em ordered set} as pair $(S,F)$, consisting of
