nodes.name: 1-Segal and 2-Segal simplicial objects
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a combinatorial model category, and let $X \in \mathbf{C}_\Delta$ be a simplicial object. \begin{enumerate} \item We say that $X$ is {\em 1-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 1$, the morphism \[ f_n: X_n \longrightarrow (I[n], X)_R = X_1\times^R_{X_0} X_1 \times^R_{X_0} \cdots \times^R_{X_0} X_1, \] induced by the embedding $I[n] \hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. \item We say that $X$ is {\em 2-Segal} if, for every $n\geq 2$ and every triangulation $\mathcal{T}$ of $P_{n+1}$, the morphism \[ f_{\mathcal{T}}: X_n \longrightarrow (\Delta^{\mathcal{T}}, X)_R, \] induced by the embedding $\Delta^{\mathcal{T}}\hookrightarrow \Delta^n$, is a weak equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. \end{enumerate}
nodes.label: def:segal

nodes.name: Underived Segal conditions
nodes.statement: Let $\mathbf{C}$ be an ordinary category with limits and colimits. We can equip $\mathbf{C}$ with the trivial model structure such that the weak equivalences are given by the class of isomorphisms. The above Segal conditions then involve underived membrane spaces require the corresponding morphisms $f_n$, respectively $f_{\mathcal{T}}$, to be isomorphisms in $\mathbf{C}$.

nodes.name: $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-set realization of a graph
nodes.statement: Given a ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graph $\Gamma$, the limit of the associated diagram $I(\Gamma) \to ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}$, denoted by ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$, is called the {\em ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set realization of $\Gamma$}.

nodes.name: Functoriality of the $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-set realization
nodes.statement: The ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set realization extends to a functor \[ {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}. \]
conclusions: The ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-set realization extends to a functor

nodes.name: Proof of Functoriality of the $\Delta\mathfrak{G}$-set realization
nodes.statement: A morphism $\varphi$ between ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ consists of a functor $\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories together with a natural transformation $\eta: \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \circ \varphi \to \widetilde{I}_\Gamma$. We obtain a canonical sequence of morphisms \[ \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \longrightarrow \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \varphi \overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow} \lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma} \] whose composite defines the desired morphism ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma'} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$. Here the first morphism is the natural morphism $\lim F \to \lim F \varphi$ which exists for any functor $F: I(\Gamma') \to \mathbf{C}$ provided that both limits exist. It is straightforward to verify the functoriality of this association.
nodes.statement_short: A morphism of structured graphs gives a canonical map of limits.

nodes.name: Unpack a morphism of structured graphs.
nodes.statement:
A morphism $\varphi$ between ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs $\Gamma$ and $\Gamma'$ consists of a functor
	$\varphi: I(\Gamma) \to I(\Gamma')$ of incidence categories together with 
	a natural transformation $\eta: \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \circ \varphi \to
	\widetilde{I}_\Gamma$.
nodes.statement_short: Unpack a morphism of structured graphs.

nodes.name: Compose canonical maps of limits.
nodes.statement:
We obtain a canonical sequence of morphisms
	\[
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \longrightarrow 
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma'} \varphi \overset{\eta}{\longrightarrow}
		\lim \Upsilon D \widetilde{I}_{\Gamma}
	\]
	whose composite defines the desired morphism ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma'} \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}$.
nodes.statement_short: Compose canonical maps of limits.

nodes.name: The first map exists for any functor; functoriality is direct.
nodes.statement:
Here the first
	morphism is the natural morphism $\lim F \to \lim F \varphi$ which exists for any
	functor $F: I(\Gamma') \to \mathbf{C}$ provided that both limits exist. It is straightforward to
	verify the functoriality of this association.
nodes.statement_short: The first map exists for any functor; functoriality is direct.

nodes.name: Functor $RX$
nodes.statement:
Let $\mathbf{C}$ be a combinatorial model category, and let $X: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \to \mathbf{C}$ a ${\mathcal G}$-structured
$2$-Segal object in $\mathbf{C}$. We form the right homotopy Kan extension of $X$ along the Yoneda embedding 
$\Upsilon: {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{{\operatorname{op}}} \to ({\mathcal Set}_{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}})^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ and take the composite with the above functors 
to obtain a canonical functor
\begin{equation} RX: P(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C}),\; \Gamma \mapsto RX({\Gamma})
\end{equation}
where $RX(\Gamma) := R \Upsilon_*X ({\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma})$ and $\Gamma$ is equipped with its natural
${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured from Proposition \ref{prop:emb-graph-str}.

nodes.name: Functor $RX$ on spanning graphs
nodes.statement: RX: P(S,M) \longrightarrow \operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C}),\; \Gamma \mapsto RX({\Gamma})
nodes.label: eq:RX

nodes.name: Invariant $X(S,M)$
nodes.statement:
Finally, we define
\[
	X(S,M) := \varinjlim{} RX.
\]

nodes.name: Categorified structured state sum
nodes.statement: The object $X(S,M)$ comes equipped with a canonical isomorphism \begin{equation} RX({\Gamma}) \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} X(S,M), \end{equation} for every object $\Gamma$ in $P(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: For a structured 2-Segal object $X$, the invariant $X(S,M)$ is computed by $RX(\Gamma)$ for any spanning graph $\Gamma$.
conclusions: The object $X(S,M)$ comes equipped with a canonical isomorphism
nodes.label: thm:state-sum

nodes.name: State sum isomorphism
nodes.statement: RX({\Gamma}) \overset{\cong}{\longrightarrow} X(S,M),
nodes.label: eq:statesum

nodes.name: Proof of Categorified structured state sum
nodes.statement: The claimed isomorphisms are simply the maps which consitute the colimit cone under the diagram $RX$. These maps are isomorphisms since, by Theorem \ref{thm:contractible}, the diagram $RX$ is indexed by a simply connected index category and, due to the $2$-Segal property satisfied by $X$, maps all morphisms to isomorphisms in $\operatorname{Ho}(\mathbf{C})$ (see \cite{HSS-triangulated}).
nodes.statement_short: Colimit cone maps are isomorphisms since $P(S,M)$ is simply connected and the 2-Segal property inverts all morphisms.

nodes.name: Categorified state sum formula
nodes.statement: Theorem \ref{thm:state-sum} shows that the structured surface invariant $X(S,M)$ can be explicitly computed via the formula \[ X(S,M) \cong \operatorname{ho}\! \underleftarrow{\lim}{}_{\{{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^n \to {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}^{\Gamma}\}} X_n \] where $\Gamma$ is any chosen spanning graph embedded in $S$. This formula can be regarded as a categorified variant of the state sum formulas for surface invariants in the context of topological field theory.

nodes.name: Proof of Coherent mapping class group action
nodes.statement:
Consider the functor
\[
  {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}, \; \Gamma \mapsto RX(\Gamma).
\]
Due to the $2$-Segal property of $X$, it maps weak equivalences of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs to weak
equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$. We can pass to classifying spaces to obtain a map of topological spaces.
\[
  |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|
\]
where $W_{\mathbf{C}}$ denotes the category of weak equivalences in $\mathbf{C}$. By Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph}, we
have
\[
	|{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \simeq \coprod_{(S,M)} B\, \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)
\]
so that we obtain, for every stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface $(S,M)$, a map
\[
	\rho: B\, \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M) \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|.
\]
The topological space $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ is a model for the maximal $\infty$-groupoid in the simplicial
localization of $\mathbf{C}$ with respect to $W$ (cf. \cite{dwyer-kan}). Therefore, the map $\rho$ realizes
a coherent action of the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)$ on $\rho(*) \cong X(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: The 2-Segal property makes $RX$ invert weak equivalences; combine with Theorem 4.12 to get a map $B\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)\to|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$.

nodes.name: $RX$ on structured graphs inverts weak equivalences.
nodes.statement:
Consider the functor
\[
  {\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph} \longrightarrow \mathbf{C}, \; \Gamma \mapsto RX(\Gamma).
\]
Due to the $2$-Segal property of $X$, it maps weak equivalences of ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-structured graphs to weak
equivalence in $\mathbf{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: $RX$ on structured graphs inverts weak equivalences.

nodes.name: Pass to classifying spaces.
nodes.statement:
We can pass to classifying spaces to obtain a map of topological spaces.
\[
  |{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|
\]
where $W_{\mathbf{C}}$ denotes the category of weak equivalences in $\mathbf{C}$.
nodes.statement_short: Pass to classifying spaces.

nodes.name: Theorem 4.12 identifies the source with $B\operatorname{Mod}^{\math...
nodes.statement:
By Theorem \ref{thm:g-graph}, we
have
\[
	|{\Delta \mathfrak{G}}-\operatorname{Graph}| \simeq \coprod_{(S,M)} B\, \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)
\]
so that we obtain, for every stable $\mathbb{G}$-structured surface $(S,M)$, a map
\[
	\rho: B\, \operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M) \longrightarrow |W_{\mathbf{C}}|.
\]
nodes.statement_short: Theorem 4.12 identifies the source with $B\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}$.

nodes.name: Maps into $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ are coherent actions.
nodes.statement:
The topological space $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ is a model for the maximal $\infty$-groupoid in the simplicial
localization of $\mathbf{C}$ with respect to $W$ (cf. \cite{dwyer-kan}). Therefore, the map $\rho$ realizes
a coherent action of the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)$ on $\rho(*) \cong X(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Maps into $|W_{\mathbf{C}}|$ are coherent actions.

nodes.name: Coherent mapping class group action
nodes.statement: The structured mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}^{\mathbb{G}}(S,M)$ acts coherently on the object $X(S,M)$.
nodes.label: thm:mod-act

nodes.name: 2-coSegal
nodes.statement:
We say that $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal if $\mathscr{F}^{{\operatorname{op}}}$ is $2$-Segal and translate
all other concepts in a similar way.

nodes.name: Fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$
nodes.statement:
Given a marked unoriented surface $(S,M)$,
we define the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ to be the groupoid with set of objects $M$ and
morphisms given by homotopy classes of paths in $S$ between points in $M$.

nodes.name: Codihedral fundamental groupoid
nodes.statement:
Consider the codihedral groupoid
\[
	\mathscr{F}: \Xi \longrightarrow {\bf Grpds}, \; [n] \mapsto \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots,n\})
\]
where $\Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\})$ denotes the fundamental groupoid of the unit disk $D$ in $\mathbb{C}$, relative
to the subset $\{0,1,\dots,n\} \subset D$ of $(n+1)$st roots of unity.

nodes.name: Fundamental groupoids from the disk
nodes.statement: The codihedral groupoid $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal. The value $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ of $\mathscr{F}$ on an unoriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative to $M$.
conclusions: is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative
nodes.label: prop:kampen

nodes.name: Proof of Fundamental groupoids from the disk
nodes.statement: To verify the $2$-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the $n+1$-gon $P_n$ into two polygons $P_m$ with vertices $\{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}$ and $P_l$ with vertices $\{i,i+1,\dots, j\}$, the corresponding functor \[ f: \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}) \coprod_{\Pi_1(D, \{i,j\})} \Pi_1(D, \{i,i+1,\dots, j\}) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\}) \] is an isomorphism of groupoids. Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe $f$ as the natural functor \[ f': \Pi_1(P_m) \coprod_{\Pi_1(P_1)} \Pi_1(P_l) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(P_n) \] induced from expressing $P_n$ as the union of $P_m$ and $P_l$ with intersection $P_m \cap P_l = P_1$. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective polygon. The fact that $f'$ is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem (see, e.g., \cite[6.7.2]{brown}). Similarly, to compute $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$, note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in $S \setminus M$ to express $(S,M)$ as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula \eqref{eq:statesum} in these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ is the fundamental groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of $(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: 2-Segal gluing and the evaluation on surfaces are both instances of van Kampen's theorem for polygonal decompositions.

nodes.name: Reduce 2-Segal to gluing two polygons.
nodes.statement:
To verify the $2$-Segal property, we have to show that, for any subdivision of the $n+1$-gon $P_n$
into two polygons $P_m$ with vertices $\{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}$ and $P_l$ with vertices
$\{i,i+1,\dots, j\}$, the corresponding functor
\[
	f: \Pi_1(D, \{0,1,\dots, i, j, j+1, \dots, n\}) \coprod_{\Pi_1(D, \{i,j\})} \Pi_1(D, \{i,i+1,\dots, j\}) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(D,\{0,1,\dots,n\})
\]
is an isomorphism of groupoids.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce 2-Segal to gluing two polygons.

nodes.name: Rewrite via fundamental groupoids of polygons.
nodes.statement:
Up to isomorphism of groupoids we can alternatively describe $f$
as the natural functor
\[
	f': \Pi_1(P_m) \coprod_{\Pi_1(P_1)} \Pi_1(P_l) \longrightarrow \Pi_1(P_n)
\]
induced from expressing $P_n$ as the union of $P_m$ and $P_l$ with intersection $P_m \cap P_l =
P_1$. Here, all fundamental groupoids are taken with respect to the vertices of the respective
polygon.
nodes.statement_short: Rewrite via fundamental groupoids of polygons.

nodes.name: Van Kampen's theorem.
nodes.statement:
The fact that $f'$ is an isomorphism of groupoids is an easy instance of van Kampen's theorem
(see, e.g., \cite[6.7.2]{brown}).
nodes.statement_short: Van Kampen's theorem.

nodes.name: Evaluate on a polygonal decomposition by van Kampen.
nodes.statement:
Similarly, to compute $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$, note that we can pass to the dual of a spanning graph in $S
\setminus M$ to express $(S,M)$ as a union of polygons. Interpreting formula \eqref{eq:statesum} in
these terms, another application of van Kampen's theorem shows that $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ is the fundamental
groupoid $\Pi_1(S,M)$ computed as a colimit parametrized by the above polygonal subdivision of
$(S,M)$.
nodes.statement_short: Evaluate on a polygonal decomposition by van Kampen.

nodes.name: Abelian groups $\mathscr{F}_n$
nodes.statement:
For $n \ge 0$, we define the abelian group $\mathscr{F}_n$ to be
the kernel of the homomorphism
\[
	\mathbb{Z}^{n+1} \to \mathbb{Z},\; (z_0,z_1,\dots,z_n) \mapsto \sum z_i.
\]

nodes.name: Codihedral abelian group of relative homology
nodes.statement:
These abelian groups organize into a codihedral abelian group
\[
	\mathscr{F}: \Xi \longrightarrow \mathbf{A}, \; [n] \mapsto \mathscr{F}_n.
\]
conclusions: These abelian groups organize into a codihedral abelian group

nodes.name: Proof of Codihedral abelian group of relative homology
nodes.statement:
This can be seen by forming a larger codihedral abelian group given as the composite
\[
	\Xi \overset{\lambda}{\longrightarrow} {\mathcal Set} \longrightarrow \mathbf{A}
\]
and verifying that $\mathscr{F}$ is a codihedral subgroup. Here, $\lambda$ denotes the functor from
Proposition \ref{prop:forget} and ${\mathcal Set} \to \mathbf{A}$ is the functor of taking the free abelian group
on a set.
nodes.statement_short: Realize $\mathscr{F}$ as a codihedral subgroup of the free abelian group on $\lambda$.

nodes.name: Relative homology from the disk
nodes.statement: The codihedral abelian group $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal. The value $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ of $\mathscr{F}$ on an unoriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is the relative homology $H_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative to $M$.
conclusions: is the relative homology $H_1(S,M)$ of $S$ relative

nodes.name: Proof of Relative homology from the disk
nodes.statement: Note that $\mathscr{F}_n$ can be intepreted as the relative homology of the pair $(D,\{0,1,\dots,\})$ from \S \ref{sec:fundamental}. The argument is now very similar to the proof of Proposition \ref{prop:kampen}, using the Mayer-Vietoris sequence instead of van Kampen's theorem.
nodes.statement_short: As in Proposition 5.10, with Mayer-Vietoris replacing van Kampen.

nodes.name: Matrix factorizations form a 2-coSegal cocyclic dg category
nodes.statement:
In \cite{HSS-triangulated}, we constructed a cocyclic differential 
$\mathbb{Z}/2\mathbb{Z}$-graded category
\[
	\mathscr{F}: \Lambda \longrightarrow \operatorname{dgcat}^{(2)}_{\mathbf{k}}, \; [n] \mapsto \operatorname{MF}^{\mathbb{Z}/(n+1)}(\mathbf{k}[z], z^{n+1})
\]
and verified that $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal with respect to the Morita model structure on $\operatorname{dgcat}^{(2)}$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyckerhoff-Kapranov, Triangulated surfaces in triangulated categories
conclusions: is $2$-coSegal with respect to the Morita model structure

nodes.name: Topological coFukaya category
nodes.statement:
The value of $\mathscr{F}$ on an oriented marked surface $(S,M)$ is called the topological coFukaya category
of $(S,M)$.
nodes.origin_citation: Dyckerhoff-Kapranov, Triangulated surfaces in triangulated categories

nodes.name: $N$-cocyclic matrix factorization category
nodes.statement:
Interpolating between these examples, we can define an $N$-cocyclic differential $\mathbb{Z}/2N$-graded category
\[
	\mathscr{F}_{N}: \Lambda_{N} \longrightarrow \operatorname{dgcat}_{\mathbf{k}}^{(2N)}, \;,  [n] \mapsto \operatorname{MF}^{\mathbb{Z}/N(n+1)}(\mathbf{k}[z], z^{n+1})
\]
so that $\mathscr{F}_N(S,M)$ provides a $\mathbb{Z}/2N$-graded variant of the topological coFukaya category
associated to any marked $N$-spin surface $(S,M)$.

nodes.name: Proof of Structured nerves are 2-coSegal
nodes.statement: An argument similar to \cite[7.5]{HSS1} can be used to prove the following statement.
nodes.statement_short: Argue as in Higher Segal spaces I, 7.5 (sketch).

nodes.name: Structured nerves are 2-coSegal
nodes.statement: The ${\Delta \mathfrak{G}}$-object $\mathscr{F}$ is $2$-coSegal.

nodes.name: Intrinsic interpretation of $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$
nodes.statement:
The
question of finding a general intrinsic interpretation of $\mathscr{F}(S,M)$ in terms of the $\mathbb{G}$-structured
surface is open.

nodes.name: Tessellation of a polygon
nodes.statement: A {\em tessellation} of $P$ is a (possibly empty) set of non-intersecting diagonals in $P$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Poset $\operatorname{Tess}(P)$
nodes.statement:
The set $\operatorname{Tess}(P)$ of tesselations of $P$ is partially ordered by inclusions of
 sets of diagonals.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Notation $P'\in\mathcal{P}$
nodes.statement: We write (allowing a slight abuse of notation) $P'\in\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Stasheff polytope
nodes.statement:
As well known, there is a convex polytope ${\mathbb{T}}(P)$ canonically associated to $P$
 and called the {\em Stasheff polytope} of $P$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Faces of the Stasheff polytope
nodes.statement:
The poset of faces of ${\mathbb{T}}(P)$ is
 anti-isomorphic with $\operatorname{Tess}(P)$. Thus, vertices of ${\mathbb{T}}(P)$ correspond to triangulations 
 and edges to tesselations into all triangles and one 4-gon. The face of ${\mathbb{T}}(P)$ corresponding
 to a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$, is identified with
 \[
 {\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P}) \,\, := \,\, \prod_{P'\in\mathcal{P}}{\mathbb{T}}(P'). 
 \]
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Stasheff polytope of a dihedral ordinal
nodes.statement:
This means that we can associate a Stasheff polytope ${\mathbb{T}}_M$ to any finite dihedral ordinal
 $M\in\bf\Xi$, $|M|\geq 3$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Curvilinear polygon
nodes.statement:
More generally, by a {\em (curvilinear) polygon} we will mean a stable marked
 surface $(S,M)$ such that $S$ is, topologically,  a disk and $M\subset\partial S$. In  this
 case $M$ has a canonical dihedral order and we associate to $(S,M)$ the
 Stasheff polytope ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M):= {\mathbb{T}}_M$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Arc
nodes.statement:
Let now $(S,M)$ be an arbitrary stable marked surface. Following \cite{harer, fomin-shapiro-thurston},
 we call an {\em arc} on $(S,M)$ an isotopy class of unoriented paths $\gamma$ beginning
 and ending on $M$ (possibly at the same point) such that:
 \begin{enumerate}
 \item[(1)] $\gamma$ does not meet any  elements of $M$ other than containing them as endpoints.
 
 \item[(2)] $\gamma$ does not have any self-intersection points  except possibly endpoints which
 coincide. 
 
 \item[(3)] $\gamma$ is not homotopic (rel. endpoints) to a point, nor to a boundary segment
 between two adjacent marked points. 
 
 \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Set of arcs
nodes.statement:
We denote by $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$ the set of arcs for $(S,M)$. Thus, in the case when $(S,M)$ is a polygon, $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$
 is identified with the set of diagonals.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Sub-tessellation
nodes.statement:
A {\em sub-tesselation} (or an {\em arc system}) of $(S,M)$ is a finite subset $\mathcal{P}\subset \mathcal{A}(S,M)$ which can
 be represented by a system of pairwise non-intersecting paths.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Tessellation of a marked surface
nodes.statement: A {\em tessellation} of $(S,M)$ is a sub-tesselation $\mathcal{P}$ such that each $(S'_i, M'_i)\in\mathcal{P}$ is a polygon. For a tesselation $\mathcal{P}$ we define its Stasheff polytope as the product \[ {\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P}) \,\,=\,\, \prod_{(S', M')\in\mathcal{P}} {\mathbb{T}}(S', M'). \]
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Poset of tessellations and triangulations
nodes.statement:
The set $\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$ of tesselations of $(S,M)$ is partially ordered by inclusion of subsets in
 $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$. Maximal elements are {\em triangulations} of $(S,M)$: tesselations for which
 each $(S',M')$ is a triangle, i.e., $|M'|=3$, $M'\subset\partial S'$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Tessellation complex
nodes.statement: The {\em tessellation complex} ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is a polyhedral complex obtained by gluing the polytopes ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ for all $\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$ using the face embeddings ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P}')\hookrightarrow {\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ for $\mathcal{P}\leq\mathcal{P}'$>
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Dual graph of a tessellation
nodes.statement:
Given a tessellation $\mathcal{P}\in\operatorname{Tess}(S,M)$, we associate to it its {\em dual graph} $\Gamma_{\mathcal{P}}$
 by putting one vertex $v_{S',M'}$ inside  each polygon $(S',M')\in\mathcal{P}$ and connected the
 adjacent $v_{(S',M')}$ be edges, similarly to \cite[\S 3.3.3]{HSS-triangulated}.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Proof of Tessellation complex and spanning graphs
nodes.statement:
When $\mathcal{P}$ varies,
 the $\Gamma_{\mathcal{P}}$ run over all isotopy classes of spanning graphs for $(S,M)$.
 This implies the following.
nodes.statement_short: Dual graphs of tessellations run over all spanning graphs, so the tessellation complex models the nerve of $P(S,M)$.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Tessellation complex and spanning graphs
nodes.statement: ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the category $P(S,M)$. \qed
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
conclusions: is homotopy equivalent to the nerve of the category $P(S,M)$.
nodes.label: prop:tess-graph

nodes.name: Contractibility of the tessellation complex
nodes.statement: For any stable marked surface $(S,M)$ (orientable or not) the tessellation complex ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is contractible.
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex
assumptions: For any stable marked surface $(S,M)$ (orientable or not)
nodes.label: thm:contractible

nodes.name: Proof of Contractibility of the tessellation complex
nodes.statement:
Similarly to the oriented case, the proof can be extracted from the results of Harer \cite{harer},
  suitably adjusted,  as we now explain.
nodes.statement_short: Adapt Harer's results to the unoriented case (carried out in A.2-A.3).
nodes.section: The Stasheff polytopes and the tessellation complex

nodes.name: Simplicial complex
nodes.statement:
By a {\em (regular) simplicial complex}  we will mean a datum $A=(V,\Sigma)$
 where $V$ is a set whose elements are called {\em vertices} of $A$, and $\Sigma\subset 2^V$
 is a family of finite subsets called {\em simplices} of $A$. It is required that:
 \begin{itemize}
 \item All 1-element subsets of $V$ are in $\Sigma$.
 
 \item If $I\in \Sigma$ and $I'\subset I$, then $I'\in\Sigma$. 
 \end{itemize}
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Realization of a simplicial complex
nodes.statement:
The {\em realization} $|A|$ of a simplicial complex $X$ is obtained in a standard way by
 gluing the geometric simplices $\Delta^I$ associated to $I\in\Sigma$. Explicitly,
 \[
 \Delta^I \,\,=\,\,\left\{ (p_a)_{a\in I}\in\mathbb{R}^I \bigl| \,\, p_a\geq 0, \,\,\sum_{a\in I} p_a =1\right\}. 
 \]
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Simplicial subcomplex
nodes.statement:
A {\em simplicial subcomplex} of $A=(V,\Sigma)$ is a simplicial complex $A'=(V',\Sigma')$
 s.t. $V'\subset V$ and $\Sigma'\subset\Sigma$. In this case $|A'|$ is a closed subset of $|A|$.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Space
nodes.statement:
By a {\em space} we will always mean a topological space homeomorphic to $|A|-|A'|$ where
 $A$ is a simplicial complex and $A'\subset A$ is a subcomplex.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Classical and monotone nerves
nodes.statement: (a) Let $X$ be a space and $\mathcal{U} = (U_a)_{a\in V}$ be a locally finite covering of $X$ by closed subspaces $U_a$. The {\em classical nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}=(V, \Sigma)$ where $\Sigma$ consists of finite $I\subset V$ s.t. $\bigcap_{v\in I} U_v\neq\emptyset$. \vskip .2cm (b) In the situation (a), assume that the covering $\mathcal{U}$ is {\em saturated}, i.e., for any $U,U'\in \mathcal{U}$ the intersection $U\cap U'$ is either empty or belongs to $\mathcal{U}$. The {\em monotone nerve} of $\mathcal{U}$ is the simplicial complex $\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U} = (V.\Sigma^\leq)$, where $\Sigma^\leq$ consists of $I=\{v_0, \cdots, v_p\}\subset V$ such that $U_{v_{s(0)}}\subset U_{v_{s(1)}} \subset \cdots\subset U_{v_{s(p)}}$ for some permutation $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$. Thus $|\operatorname{N}^\leq(\mathcal{U})|$ is the geometric realization of the simplicial set, given by the nerve of the poset of nonempty $U\in\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Nerve theorem
nodes.statement: \begin{enumerate} \item[(a)] Assume that any finite intersection $U_{v_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{v_p}$ is either empty or contractible. Then $|\operatorname{N}\mathcal{U}|$ is homotopy equivalent to $X$. \item[(b)] If, moreover, $\mathcal{U}$ is saturated, then $|\operatorname{N}^\leq \mathcal{U}|$ is homotopy equivalent to $X$. \qed \end{enumerate}
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold
assumptions: Assume that any finite intersection $U_{v_0}\cap\cdots\cap U_{v_p}$ is either
nodes.label: prop:nerve-classical

nodes.name: Barycentric subdivision
nodes.statement:
The {\em barycentric subdivision} of a simplicial complex $A=(V,\Sigma)$ is the simplicial complex
 $\operatorname{Bar}(A)=(V_{\operatorname{Bar}},\Sigma_{\operatorname{Bar}})$, where $V_{\operatorname{Bar}}=\Sigma$ and $\Sigma_{\operatorname{Bar}}$ consists of finite subsets
 $\{I_0, \cdots, I_p\}$ such that $I_{s(0)} \subset I_{s(1)} \subset \cdots\subset I_{s(p)}$ 
for some permutation
  $s$ of $\{0,1,\cdots, p\}$. As well known, $|{\operatorname{Bar}}(A)|$ is canonically homeomorphic to $|A|$.
  Notationally, it will be convenient for us to think that vertices of ${\operatorname{Bar}}(A)$ are formal
  symbols  ${\operatorname{bar}}(I)$ for $I\in\Sigma$.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Link of a simplex
nodes.statement:
For each simplex $I\in\Sigma$ we have the sub complex $A_I\subset{\operatorname{Bar}}(A)$ called the
  {\em link} of $I$. By definition, $A_I=(V_I, \Sigma_I)$, where
  \[
  V_I \,\,=\,\,\bigl\{ {\operatorname{bar}}(J)\bigl| \,\, J\supset I,\,\, J\in\Sigma \bigr\}, \quad 
  \Sigma_I \,\,=\,\, \bigl\{ \{ {\operatorname{bar}}(J_0), \cdots, {\operatorname{bar}}(J_p)\}, \,\,\, I\subset J_0\subset\cdots \subset J_p\bigr\}. 
  \]
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Dual subcomplex
nodes.statement:
If $A'$ is a subcomplex of $A$ as above, we define the {\em dual subcomplex} to $(A,A')$
  as
  \[
  (A,A')^\vee \,\,=\,\,\bigcup_{I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'} A_I \,\,\,\subset \,\,\, {\operatorname{Bar}}(A). 
  \]
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Dual subcomplex models the complement
nodes.statement: The realization $|(A,A')^\vee|$ is homotopy equivalent to $|A|-|A'|$.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold
nodes.label: prop:dual-CW

nodes.name: Proof of Dual subcomplex models the complement
nodes.statement: We consider the covering $\mathcal{U}$ of $|A|-|A'|$ by closed subsets $\Delta^I_0 = \Delta^I \cap (|A|-|A'|)$ for $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$. This covering is saturated, and $(A,A')^\vee=\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U}$. As each $\Delta^I_0$ is contractible, our statement follows from Proposition \ref{prop:nerve-classical}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Cover the complement by contractible saturated pieces and apply the nerve theorem.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Saturated cover whose monotone nerve is the dual complex.
nodes.statement:
We consider the covering $\mathcal{U}$ of  $|A|-|A'|$ by closed subsets $\Delta^I_0 =
  \Delta^I \cap (|A|-|A'|)$ for $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$. This covering is saturated, and $(A,A')^\vee=\operatorname{N}^\leq\mathcal{U}$.
nodes.statement_short: Saturated cover whose monotone nerve is the dual complex.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Apply the nerve theorem.
nodes.statement:
As each $\Delta^I_0$ is contractible, our statement follows from Proposition 
  \ref{prop:nerve-classical}. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Apply the nerve theorem.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Triangulated manifold and dual cells
nodes.statement:
By a {\em triangulated manifold} we mean a pair $(A, A')$ consisting of a simplicial complex $A$ and
  a subcomplex $A'$ such that $|A|-|A'|$ is a topological manifold. In this case each $|A_I|$, $I\in\Sigma-\Sigma'$,
  is a topological cell which we call the {\em dual cell} to $I$. Thus $|(A,A')^\vee|$ is equipped with a cell
  decomposition with cells $|A_I|$.
nodes.section: The dual cell complex of a triangulated manifold

nodes.name: Arc complex
nodes.statement:
Let $(S,M)$ be a stable marked surface. The {\em arc complex} $A=A(S,M)$ is the
  simplicial complex with the set of vertices $\mathcal{A}(S,M)$ and simplices being sub-tesselations.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Subcomplex $A_\infty$
nodes.statement: It has a subcomplex $A_\infty=A_\infty(S,M)$ formed by sub-tesselations which are not tesselations.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Tessellation complex as dual complex
nodes.statement: The tessellation complex ${\mathbb{T}}(S,M)$ is homeomorphic to $|(A, A_\infty)^\vee|$ so that each cell ${\mathbb{T}}(\mathcal{P})$ is identified with $A_{\mathcal{P}}$, the link of $\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.label: prop:tess-A

nodes.name: Proof of Tessellation complex as dual complex
nodes.statement: Clear by comparing the definitions. \qed
nodes.statement_short: Compare the definitions.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Harer's triangulation of Teichmüller space
nodes.statement: There is a homeomorphism $\Psi=\Psi_{S,M}: |A|-|A_\infty| \to \operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$, equivariant with respect to the mapping class group $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
nodes.label: thm:harer-triang

nodes.name: Proof of Harer's triangulation of Teichmüller space
nodes.statement: The construction and the argument of \cite{harer} extend to the general case as follows. A point $p\in |A|-|A_\infty|$ lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex $\Delta^{\mathcal{P}}$ for some tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates \[ (p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}, \,\, p_\gamma > 0,\,\, \sum p_\gamma = 1, \] one for each arc $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}$. Consider a polygon $(S'_i, M'_i)$ of $\mathcal{P}$. To each edge $e$ of $S'_i$ we associate the ``length" $p_e:=p_\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the arc of $\mathcal{P}$ that gave rise to $e$. Let $l_e=\sum_{e\subset\partial S'_i} p_e$ be the total ``length" of $\partial S'_i$. Let $S''_i$ be a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with center $0$ and circumference $l_e$. We can map $M'_i$ bijectively to a subset $M''_i\subset \partial S''_i$ so that the distances (on $\partial S''_i$) between neighboring elements of $M''_i$ match the corresponding numbers $p_e$ for the edges of $S'_i$. In this way we get a stable marked Klein surface $(S''_i, M''_i)$. We now glue the $(S''_i, M''_i)$ together in the same fashion as the $(S'_i, M'_i)$ are glued together to form $(S, M)$. For this, we use the identifications of the boundary arcs of different $S''_i$ which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length) coordinates on the circles $\partial S''_i$. In this way we get a Klein surface $(S'', M'')$, identified with $(S,M)$ by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$. This defines the map $\Psi_{S,M}$. Its $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-equivariance is clear. The fact that $\Psi_{S,M}$ is a homeomorphism, was proved in \cite{harer} in the oriented case. Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, and let $\varpi: (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)\to (S,M)$ be its orientation cover, with the deck involution $\tau$ preserving $\widetilde M$. By equivariance, the homeomorphism \[ \Psi_{\widetilde S, \widetilde M}: \,\, |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)| \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich} (\widetilde S, \widetilde M) \] sends the involution $\tau_A: |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\to |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|$ induced by $\tau$, to $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$. Because of Proposition \ref{thm:klein-teich}(b2), we are reduced to the following.
nodes.statement_short: Build a Klein surface from barycentric coordinates by gluing disks with arc lengths; the non-orientable case reduces via the orientation cover to Lemma A.10.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Extend Harer's construction.
nodes.statement: The construction and the argument of \cite{harer}  extend to the general case as follows.
nodes.statement_short: Extend Harer's construction.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Barycentric coordinates on arcs.
nodes.statement:
A point $p\in |A|-|A_\infty|$ lies, by definition, strictly inside a simplex $\Delta^{\mathcal{P}}$ for some
  tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ and thus is represented by the collection of its barycentric coordinates
  \[
  (p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}, \,\, p_\gamma > 0,\,\, \sum p_\gamma = 1,
  \]
  one for each arc $\gamma\in\mathcal{P}$.
nodes.statement_short: Barycentric coordinates on arcs.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Edge lengths of the polygons.
nodes.statement:
Consider a polygon $(S'_i, M'_i)$ of $\mathcal{P}$. To each edge $e$ of $S'_i$ we associate the ``length"
  $p_e:=p_\gamma$ where $\gamma$ is the arc of $\mathcal{P}$ that gave rise to $e$. Let $l_e=\sum_{e\subset\partial S'_i} p_e$
  be the total ``length" of $\partial S'_i$.
nodes.statement_short: Edge lengths of the polygons.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Glue round disks with matching lengths to get a Klein surface.
nodes.statement:
Let $S''_i$ be a disk in $\mathbb{C}$ with center $0$ and circumference $l_e$. We can map $M'_i$ bijectively
  to a subset $M''_i\subset \partial S''_i$ so that the distances (on $\partial S''_i$) between neighboring
  elements of $M''_i$ match the corresponding numbers $p_e$ for the edges of $S'_i$. In this way we
  get
  a stable marked Klein surface $(S''_i, M''_i)$. We now glue the $(S''_i, M''_i)$ together in the same
  fashion as the $(S'_i, M'_i)$ are glued together to form $(S, M)$. For this, we use the identifications
  of the boundary arcs of different $S''_i$ which are affine linear in the standard angle (or arc length)
  coordinates on the circles $\partial S''_i$. In this way we get a Klein surface $(S'', M'')$, identified with
  $(S,M)$ by a diffeomorphism unique up to isotopy. In other words, we get a point of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$.
  This defines the map $\Psi_{S,M}$. Its $\operatorname{Mod}(S,M)$-equivariance is clear.
nodes.statement_short: Glue round disks with matching lengths to get a Klein surface.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Harer's oriented case.
nodes.statement: The fact that $\Psi_{S,M}$ is a homeomorphism, was proved in \cite{harer} in the oriented case.
nodes.statement_short: Harer's oriented case.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Reduce via the orientation cover to Lemma A.10.
nodes.statement:
Suppose $S$ is non-orientable, and let $\varpi: (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)\to (S,M)$
  be its orientation cover, with the deck involution $\tau$ preserving $\widetilde M$.
  By equivariance, the homeomorphism
  \[
  \Psi_{\widetilde S, \widetilde M}: \,\, |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)| 
  \longrightarrow \operatorname{Teich} (\widetilde S, \widetilde M)
  \]
  sends  the involution $\tau_A: |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\to |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|$
  induced by $\tau$,  to $\tau_{\operatorname{Teich}}$.
  Because of Proposition \ref{thm:klein-teich}(b2), we are reduced to the following.
nodes.statement_short: Reduce via the orientation cover to Lemma A.10.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Fixed points of the deck involution on the arc complex
nodes.statement: We have \[ \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A} \,\,=\,\, |A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|. \]
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Proof of Fixed points of the deck involution on the arc complex
nodes.statement:
A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies
  in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant
  sub-tesselation $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of
  arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$. 
  We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not
  meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$
  does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy  between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and 
  $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either
  $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering).
  So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation. 
  
  Further, suppose that $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$
  of $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. 
  Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation. 
  
  We conclude that 
  \[
  p\,\,\in \,\,  \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A}
  \]
  must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ where $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$
  is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates
  $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections
  of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates
  $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the
  simplex $\Delta^{\mathcal{P}}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem 
  \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant sub-tessellations of the orientation cover descend to sub-tessellations, tessellations to tessellations, and invariant barycentric coordinates match those downstairs.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Invariant simplex and its image arcs.
nodes.statement:
A point $p\in |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|^{\tau_A}$ lies
  in a $\tau$-invariant simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ corresponding to a $\tau$-invariant
  sub-tesselation $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ of $(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)$. Let $\mathcal{P}$ be the set of
  arcs $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$, $\widetilde\gamma\in\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant simplex and its image arcs.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Image is a sub-tessellation
nodes.statement:
We claim that $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation for $(S,M)$. Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not
  meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$
  does not intersect itself. Further, a homotopy  between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and 
  $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either
  $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering).
  So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation.
nodes.statement_short: Claim: the image arcs form a sub-tessellation.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Disjointness from the translate gives no self-intersection.
nodes.statement:
Indeed, the fact that $\widetilde \gamma$ does not
  meet $\tau(\widetilde \gamma)$ (which both belong to $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$) means that $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma)$
  does not intersect itself.
nodes.statement_short: Disjointness from the translate gives no self-intersection.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Distinct arcs stay non-homotopic.
nodes.statement:
Further, a homotopy  between $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_1)$ and 
  $\varpi(\widetilde\gamma_2)$ implies that that $\widetilde \gamma_2$ is homotopic to either
  $\widetilde \gamma_1$ or to $\tau(\widetilde \gamma_1)$ (because $\varpi$ is an unramified covering).
  So $\mathcal{P}$ is a sub-tesselation.
nodes.statement_short: Distinct arcs stay non-homotopic.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Tessellations descend to tessellations.
nodes.statement:
Further, suppose that $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ is a tessellation, Then any polygon $(\widetilde S'_i, \widetilde M'_i)$
  of $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}$ must be an unramified covering of its image which therefore must also be a polygon. 
  Therefore $\mathcal{P}$ is a tessellation.
nodes.statement_short: Tessellations descend to tessellations.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Invariant coordinates match coordinates downstairs.
nodes.statement:
We conclude that 
  \[
  p\,\,\in \,\,  \bigl( |A(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|-|A_\infty(\widetilde S, \widetilde M)|\bigr)^{\tau_A}
  \]
  must lie in a simplex $\Delta^{\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ where $\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}=\varpi^{-1}(\mathcal{P})$
  is the preimage of a tessellation $\mathcal{P}$ of $(S,M)$ and be given by a collection of barycentric coordinates
  $(p_{\widetilde\gamma})_{{\widetilde\gamma}\in\widetilde{\mathcal{P}}}$ which is $\tau$-invariant. Such collections
  of coordinates are in bijection (homeomorphism) with collections of barycentric coordinates
  $(p_\gamma)_{\gamma\in\mathcal{P}}$, $\sum p_\gamma=1$, i.e., with points of the
  simplex $\Delta^{\mathcal{P}}$ in $|A(S,M)| - |A_\infty(S,M)|$. This proves the lemma and Theorem 
  \ref{thm:harer-triang}.
nodes.statement_short: Invariant coordinates match coordinates downstairs.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space

nodes.name: Proof of Contractibility of the spanning graph poset
nodes.statement:
Now, Propositions \ref{prop:tess-graph},  \ref{prop:tess-A} and \ref{prop:dual-CW} together with the fact that
  $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$ is homeomorphic to a Euclidean space (Theorem \ref{thm:klein-teich}(c))
  imply Theorem \ref{thm:graph-contr}.
nodes.statement_short: Combine Propositions A.3, A.8, A.7 with contractibility of $\operatorname{Teich}(S,M)$.
nodes.section: Harer's triangulation of the Teichm\"uller space
